會試錄序

嘉靖壬辰春二月，天下士前後舉于鄉及署教限年者，凡三千八百餘人，咸集試于禮部。先事，尚書臣夏言、侍郎臣湛若水、臣顧鼎臣疏謂：「文體比多舛異，宜申勅主司慎所去取，為程式以風四方。翰林儒臣裁數人，或備講筵侍從，宜增選省署之臣與同事。」詔可。及期，請主試者，臣潮、臣維藩拜命承乏，大懼弗任，無以稱塞
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second month of spring in the renchen year of Jiajing [1532], more than 3,800 scholars from throughout the realm—those recommended in successive Provincial Examinations and those provisionally appointed to teaching posts who had completed the required term—assembled to take the examination at the Ministry of Rites. Before the examination, your servants Xia Yan, Minister of Rites, and Zhan Ruoshui and Gu Dingchen, Vice Ministers of Rites, submitted a memorial stating: “Of late, literary style has frequently become aberrant. An injunction should again be issued to the examiners to exercise care in rejecting and selecting compositions, establishing models to guide the realm. There are only a few Confucian scholars in the Hanlin Academy, some of whom serve as lecturers and attendants at the imperial lectures. Additional officials from the central government offices should be selected to work alongside them.” The emperor approved. When the appointed time arrived and a request was made for chief examiners, we, your servants Chao and Weifan, respectfully received the appointment, filling the posts for want of better men. We greatly feared that we were unequal to the task and had no means adequately to fulfill…

朝日乃
命先二日入院雖齋禁亦

編修臣衮臣衢臣文德臣名

===

題必明且正無敢困以隱僻

〔臣雲同臣邦直臣珂〕而凡試
院事則〔臣若水〕主之御史〔臣〕
〔朝用臣鳳韶〕監之及慎選諸
執事皆如例比鎖院三試命
題必明且正無敢困以隱僻
punctuated: 明詔。是月丙戌，祀朝日，乃命先二日入院。雖齋禁，亦錫寵宴如制，重求賢也。同考則侍讀臣教，修撰臣以訓、臣用卿，編修臣衮、臣衢、臣文德、臣名，都給事中臣經、臣潤身，給事中臣金、臣洪、臣繼美，署郎中臣叔嗣，署員外郎臣庭，主事臣雲同、臣邦直、臣珂。而凡試院事，則臣若水主之，御史臣朝用、臣鳳韶監之。及慎選諸執事，皆如例。比鎖院，三試命題必明且正，無敢困以隱僻。
translation_en:
…the illustrious edict. On the bingxu day of that month, the sacrifice to the Morning Sun was to be performed; an order therefore directed us to enter the examination compound two days beforehand. Despite the restrictions of ritual fasting, we were graciously bestowed a banquet according to established regulations, such was the importance attached to seeking worthy men.

The Associate Examiners were your servants Jiao, Reader-in-Waiting; Yixun and Yongqing, Senior Compilers; Gun, Qu, Wende, and Ming, Junior Compilers; Jing and Runshen, Chief Supervising Secretaries; Jin, Hong, and Jimei, Supervising Secretaries; Shusi, Acting Bureau Director; Ting, Acting Vice Director; and Yuntong, Bangzhi, and Ke, Secretaries. Your servant Ruoshui directed all affairs of the examination compound, while your servants Chaoyong and Fengshao, Investigating Censors, supervised them. The various functionaries were also carefully selected, all according to precedent.

Once the compound was sealed, the questions set for the three sessions had to be clear and proper; none of us dared to perplex candidates with obscure or recondite material…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
取文必純以實無或有浮誕
險怪者疏請
宸斷中三百二十人將錄其名氏
并刻文以
獻臣竊聞我
皇祖嘗與儒臣論易至天地養萬
物聖人養賢以及萬民因言
===
人主職在養民若所養得賢
與之共治則民皆得所養然
養賢非難知賢為難他日論
文則以明道德通世務為賢
以險怪浮藻為戒吁
聖謨洋洋知言知人何以易此蓋
自

自
punctuated: 取文必純以實，無或有浮誕險怪者。疏請宸斷，中三百二十人，將錄其名氏，并刻文以獻。臣竊聞我皇祖嘗與儒臣論《易》，至「天地養萬物，聖人養賢以及萬民」，因言：「人主職在養民，若所養得賢，與之共治，則民皆得所養。然養賢非難，知賢為難。」他日論文，則以明道德、通世務為賢，以險怪浮藻為戒。吁！聖謨洋洋，知言知人，何以易此？蓋自
translation_en:
…In selecting essays, we required purity and substance, admitting none that were frivolous, extravagant, outlandish, or bizarre. We submitted a memorial requesting Your Majesty’s decision, and 320 men were selected. We shall record their names and have their essays printed for presentation to Your Majesty.
Your servant has heard that our Imperial Ancestor once discussed the Book of Changes with his Confucian ministers. Upon reaching the passage, “Heaven and earth nourish the myriad things; the sage nourishes worthy men and thereby extends nourishment to all the people,” he remarked: “The ruler’s duty lies in nourishing the people. If those whom he supports are worthy, and he governs together with them, then all the people will receive the nourishment they need. Yet supporting worthy men is not difficult; recognizing them is difficult.” On another occasion, when discussing writing, he deemed worthy those who illuminated the Way and virtue and understood the affairs of the world, and warned against outlandishness, eccentricity, and empty ornament. Ah! How ample is this sagely counsel! For understanding words and recognizing men, what could surpass it? For, ever since…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
天造草昧首務學校選舉未有定
制乃洪武甲子重議條格始
三歲一行罷前代詞賦陋習
而專經義論策詔誥表判之
文正欲觀體用之學期得真
賢以資治道焉耳越廿有七
載奎璧之間宿翳消滅我
===
皇祖察天象之有異卜文運之當
興一時名臣碩輔勳業文章
輝映簡冊及
聖子
神孫率由
成憲垂百六十餘年耆德俊英項
背相望科目得才之效亦既

皇祖察天象之有異卜文運之當
興一時名臣碩輔勲業文章
輝暎簡冊及
===
聖子
神孫率由
成憲垂百六十餘年者德俊英頊
背相望科目得才之效亦既
punctuated: 天造草昧，首務學校，選舉未有定制。乃洪武甲子，重議條格，始三歲一行，罷前代詞賦陋習，而專經義、論、策、詔、誥、表、判之文，正欲觀體用之學，期得真賢，以資治道焉耳。越廿有七載，奎璧之間宿翳消滅。我皇祖察天象之有異，卜文運之當興。一時名臣碩輔，勳業文章，輝映簡冊。及聖子神孫率由成憲，垂百六十餘年，耆德俊英，項背相望，科目得才之效亦既
translation_en: … at the dynasty’s founding, when all was still unformed, the foremost task was establishing schools, and no fixed system yet governed selection for office. Then, in the jiazi year of the Hongwu reign, the regulations were reconsidered, and examinations began to be held once every three years. The inferior practices of earlier dynasties, emphasizing lyric poetry and rhapsodies, were abolished. Instead, the examinations concentrated on interpretations of the Classics, discourses, policy essays, proclamations, pronouncements, memorials, and legal judgments. The intention was precisely to assess learning in both its fundamental principles and practical application, hoping to obtain truly worthy men to assist in governing. Twenty-seven years later, the lingering obscuration between the Kui and Bi lunar lodges disappeared. Our imperial ancestor observed this unusual celestial phenomenon and discerned that literary fortunes were about to flourish. The achievements and writings of the eminent ministers and great supporting statesmen of that time shone brilliantly in the historical records. Thereafter, his sage sons and divine grandsons followed the established statutes for some hundred and sixty years and more. Elders of venerable virtue and men of outstanding talent followed one another in close succession, and the efficacy of the examination system in securing talent had already …

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
徵且遠矣或乃慮文盛已極
而渾厚正大之體視前輩若
少有異焉臣竊謂
聖天子銳意中興禮樂政教一復
國初之舊將比隆唐虞三代而
極彌綸參賛之盛登進諸士
固方大有望也豈專意於文
===
===
哉顧敷言之制遠賓興之法
廢雖孔孟觀人亦往往由是
然獨於言行之訓諄切懇至
則又慮空言無實者之無益
云爾夫進士之名昉於周而
以設科始於隋至唐宋因之
不廢如陸贄韓愈范仲淹歐

固方大有望也豈專意於文
===
弐顧數言之制遠賓興之法
廢雖孔孟觀人亦往往由是
然獨於言行之訓諄切懇至
則又慮空言無實者之無益
云爾夫進士之名昉於周而
以設科始於隋至唐宋因之
不廢如陸贄韓愈范仲淹歐
punctuated: 徵且遠矣。或乃慮文盛已極，而渾厚正大之體視前輩若少有異焉。臣竊謂，聖天子銳意中興，禮樂政教一復國初之舊，將比隆唐虞三代，而極彌綸參賛之盛，登進諸士，固方大有望也，豈專意於文哉？顧敷言之制遠，賓興之法廢，雖孔孟觀人，亦往往由是。然獨於言行之訓諄切懇至，則又慮空言無實者之無益云爾。夫進士之名昉於周，而以設科始於隋，至唐宋因之不廢，如陸贄、韓愈、范仲淹、歐
translation_en:
…have been demonstrated and have long endured. Some, however, worry that literary accomplishment has already reached its height, while its substantial, harmonious, upright, and dignified character seems somewhat different from that of earlier generations. Your servant humbly believes that the sagely Son of Heaven is intent upon a restoration, returning rites, music, government, and instruction entirely to the practices of the dynasty’s founding. He will rival the flourishing rule of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties, bringing to their fullest realization the ordering of the world and assistance in the transforming work of Heaven and Earth. There are therefore great expectations for the scholars now being advanced to office. Could literary accomplishment alone be the concern?

Yet the institution of presenting one’s words for assessment belongs to the distant past, and the practice of honoring and recommending worthy men as guests has fallen into disuse. Even Confucius and Mencius often judged people through their words. Nevertheless, their teachings concerning words and conduct were especially earnest and insistent: they were concerned that empty words without substantive deeds would be of no benefit.

The designation jinshi originated under the Zhou, while its establishment as an examination category began under the Sui. The Tang and Song continued it without interruption. Such men as Lu Zhi, Han Yu, Fan Zhongyan, and Ou…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
陽修諸名臣皆由此其選也
于時文盛之弊則亦有然者
然起衰黜浮臣固深愧二子
者之能若不負所學以天下
為己任敢遽謂今士無若人
哉庸詎知不尚有進於是而
以伊周自許者哉夫然庶無
===
負天地
國家之所以生成教養者而亦
不失天下之望且以逭主司
之責與愧詩曰追琢其章金
玉其相勉勉我王綱紀四方
況今
聖明造就之下有不翕然丕變者

聖明造就之下有不翕然丕變者
punctuated: 陽修諸名臣皆由此。其選也，于時文盛之弊，則亦有然者。然起衰黜浮，臣固深愧二子者之能。若不負所學，以天下為己任，敢遽謂今士無若人哉？庸詎知不尚有進於是而以伊周自許者哉？夫然，庶無負天地國家之所以生成教養者，而亦不失天下之望，且以逭主司之責與愧。詩曰：「追琢其章，金玉其相。勉勉我王，綱紀四方。」況今聖明造就之下，有不翕然丕變者
translation_en:
…Ouyang Xiu and the other eminent ministers all emerged through this route. In its selection of men, abuses arising from the flourishing of contemporary examination prose have indeed also occurred. Yet in reviving what has declined and rejecting superficiality, your servant feels deeply ashamed before the abilities of those two masters. As for remaining true to what they have learned and taking responsibility for all under Heaven, dare we hastily say that there are no such men among today’s scholars? How can we know that there are not still others who go further, aspiring to equal Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou?

If so, they might prove worthy of the life, nurture, instruction, and support bestowed upon them by Heaven and Earth and the state, and not disappoint the hopes of all under Heaven. They might also spare the presiding examiner blame and shame. The Book of Odes says: “Chased and carved is his ornament; gold and jade are his substance. Tirelessly our king orders and regulates the four quarters.” How much more so now, under the nurturing of our sage and enlightened sovereign: could there be any who do not join together in a great transformation…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
乎臣不佞不能風以言固宜
風之行也錄成謹序述其事
而以是說終焉
中順大夫詹事府少詹事兼
翰林院學士張潮謹序
alt_text:
乎〔臣〕不佞不能風以言固宜
風之行也錄成謹序述其事
而以是說終焉
中順大夫詹事府少詹事兼
翰林院學士張潮謹序
punctuated:
乎？臣不佞，不能風以言，固宜風之行也。錄成，謹序述其事，而以是說終焉。
中順大夫、詹事府少詹事兼翰林院學士張潮謹序。
translation_en:
…? Your servant, lacking ability, cannot inspire others through words; I should certainly inspire them through my conduct. Now that this record is complete, I respectfully recount its circumstances in this preface and conclude with these remarks.
Preface respectfully written by Zhang Chao, Grand Master of Central Compliance, Junior Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Ye Hong, Gentleman for Rendering Service and Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue, had the courtesy name Ziyuan. Registered with the Dezhou Guard and a native of Yuyao County, Zhejiang, he became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the jichou year.

Shen Jimei, Gentleman for Rendering Service and Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, had the courtesy name Zichong. He was from the Guard Battalion of Baoning Prefecture, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Gao Shusi, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Merit Titles in the Ministry of Personnel, had the courtesy name Ziye. A native of Xiangfu County, Henan, he became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year.

Zhang Ting, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Personnel in the Ministry of Personnel, had the courtesy name Zijia. A native of Jiajiang County, Sichuan, he became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year.

Lin Yuntong, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary in the Shanxi Bureau of the Ministry of Revenue, had the courtesy name Ruyu. A native of Putian County, Fujian, he became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Li Bangzhi, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary in the Shanxi Bureau of the Ministry of Justice, had the courtesy name Rusi. A native of Maoming County, Guangdong, he became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year.

Liu Ke, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary in the Shandong Bureau of the Ministry of Justice, had the courtesy name Bolu. A native of Kaizhou, in the directly administered metropolitan region, he became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year.

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Wang Chaoyong, Gentleman for Rendering Literary Service and Investigating Censor for the Henan Circuit, had the courtesy name Xingfu. A native of Longxi County, Shaanxi, he became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year.

Mao Fengshao, Gentleman for Rendering Literary Service and Investigating Censor for the Sichuan Circuit, had the courtesy name Ruicheng. A native of Macheng County, Huguang, he became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year.

Proctors:

Tu Yingjun, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Wensheng. A native of Pinghu County, Zhejiang, he became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Lü Zhang, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary in the Bureau of Receptions in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Shangde. A native of Jingmen Subprefecture, Huguang, he became a metropolitan graduate in the guiwei year.

Officials in Charge of Printing Examination Papers:

Tian Rucheng, Gentleman for Receiving Virtue and Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Shuhe. A native of Qiantang County, Zhejiang, he became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Mao Qu, Gentleman for Upright Service and Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, had the courtesy name Shize. A native of Ye County, Shandong, he became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Officials in Charge of Collecting and Safekeeping Examination Scripts:

Shi Yong, Gentleman for Rendering Service and a Drafter in the Secretariat, had the courtesy name Shengyuan. Registered in Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, and a native of Jiaxing County, Zhejiang, he became a tribute student (gongshi) in the guiyou year.

第壹塲

四書

子曰：「大哉，堯之為君也！巍巍乎！唯天為大，唯堯則之。蕩蕩乎！民無能名焉。巍巍乎！其有成功也；煥乎！其有文章。」

行而世為天下法，言而世為天下則。

謹庠序之教，申之以孝悌之義。

易

其德剛健而文明，應乎天而時行，是以元亨。

六五：鼎黃耳，金鉉，利貞。

顯道，神德行，是故可與酬酢，可與祐神矣。若夫雜物撰德，辨是與非，則非其中爻不備。

書

帝曰：「吁！臣哉，鄰哉！鄰哉，臣哉！」禹曰：「俞！」

惟學遜志，務時敏，厥修乃來。允懷于兹，道積于厥躬。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: “Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone took it as his model. So vast was he that the people could find no name for him. How lofty were his accomplishments! How brilliant were his cultural achievements!”

“In his actions he serves for generations as a model for all under Heaven; in his words he serves for generations as a standard for all under Heaven.”

“Attend carefully to instruction in the local schools, reinforcing it with the principles of filial devotion and respect for elder brothers.”

Book of Changes

“His virtue is firm and vigorous, cultured and enlightened; he responds to Heaven and acts in accordance with the times. Hence there is supreme success.”

“Six in the fifth place: the cauldron has yellow ears and a metal carrying bar. It is beneficial to remain steadfast.”

“It makes the Way manifest and renders virtuous conduct numinous. Thus one may engage in question and response with it and assist the spirits. As for bringing together the various things and discerning their qualities, and distinguishing right from wrong, these cannot be fully accomplished without the middle lines.”

Book of Documents

“The sovereign said: ‘Ah! My ministers are my close companions! My close companions are my ministers!’ Yu said: ‘Yes!’”

“In learning, keep your mind humble and strive always to be diligent; then your self-cultivation will advance. If you sincerely cherish this, the Way will accumulate within your person.”

夏，公及宋公遇于清，隱公四年。
春，王正月，城楚丘，僖公二年。秦人伐晉，文公三年。
蔡侯廬歸于蔡，陳侯吳歸于陳，昭公十三年。
諸侯會于扈，文公十七年。晉人執季孫意如以歸，昭公十三年。晉士鞅帥師侵鄭，
translation_en:
The wish is only that this may endure for ten thousand years, and that the king’s sons and grandsons may protect the people forever.
Only when one truly understands and sincerely practices the nine virtues does one dare to instruct one’s sovereign, bowing with hands joined and forehead to the ground: “O sovereign! Set the right men in your offices, as your governors, and as your arbiters: this is what makes a sovereign!”

Book of Odes
Their vermilion knee-covers shine splendidly; they shall be lords and kings of their houses.
Without conscious discernment or knowledge, he follows the Supreme Lord’s pattern.
Dignified and lofty, like a jade tablet, like a jade baton; of fine reputation and high esteem, the gracious gentleman serves as the guiding cord for the four quarters.
The royal domain extends a thousand li, where the people dwell; he establishes the boundaries of all within the four seas.

Spring and Autumn Annals
In summer, the duke met the Duke of Song at Qing. Fourth year of Duke Yin.
In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, fortifications were built at Chuqiu. Second year of Duke Xi. The men of Qin attacked Jin. Third year of Duke Wen.
Lu, Marquis of Cai, returned to Cai; Wu, Marquis of Chen, returned to Chen. Thirteenth year of Duke Zhao.
The regional lords assembled at Hu. Seventeenth year of Duke Wen. The men of Jin seized Jisun Yiru and took him back with them. Thirteenth year of Duke Zhao [?]. Shi Yang of Jin led an army to invade Zheng …

禮記
是故昔先王之制禮也，因其財物而致其義焉爾。
故樂者，審一以定和，比物以飾節，節奏合以成文，所以合和父子君臣，附親萬民也，是先王立樂之方也。
使民有父之尊，有母之親，如此而后可以為民父母矣。非至德，其孰能如此乎？
君子道人以言，而禁人以行，故言必慮其所終，而行必稽其所敝，則民謹於言而慎於行。

第貳塲

translation_en:
…and then invaded Wei. 〔Eighth year of Duke Ding.〕

Record of Rites (Liji)
Thus, when the former kings established rites in antiquity, they used the material resources available to give full expression to the appropriate meaning, and that was all.
Music, therefore, examines unity to establish harmony, coordinates things to embellish rhythm, and combines rhythms and measures to form patterns. It thereby brings fathers and sons, rulers and ministers into harmony, and binds the myriad people together in affection. This was the former kings’ method of establishing music.
Let the people regard one with the reverence due a father and the affection due a mother: only then can one become the father and mother of the people. Without consummate virtue, who could accomplish this?
The gentleman guides people through his words and restrains them through his conduct. Thus, in speaking he must consider the ultimate consequences of his words, and in acting he must examine the abuses to which his conduct might lead. Then the people will be circumspect in speech and cautious in conduct.

Second Session
Discourse

天命，撫有方夏，在位餘三十年。其神功聖德，雖累歲言之，有不能盡者矣。竊觀平日所嘗惓惓訓諭臣下，見諸《聖政記》，及著爲令典，頒行中外，垂億萬載之規者，惟教刑二事，甚切於士與民。國家甄陶萬類、培植元氣之道，亦或在此。不知與古歷代之法同乎否歟？抑有所因而損益之歟？二者相須，其果然歟？行之至今，亦有稍異而當復者乎？夫訓誥律令章程具在，諸士佩服有年，而我聖天子惇崇慎恤之意，屢形詔旨者，傳播海内久矣。其並鋪張揚厲，用彰謨烈於無窮焉。儻懷芹曝之忱，尚一言之，以爲聖德中興之助。

問：有宋中葉，賢臣眾矣，論者乃獨推司馬
translation_en:
…the Mandate of Heaven and ruled over the Chinese realm, reigning for more than thirty years. His divine achievements and sagely virtue could not be fully recounted even in years of discussion. I have respectfully considered the earnest instructions he habitually gave his ministers, as recorded in the Record of Sagely Governance (Shengzheng ji), and those set down as authoritative statutes, promulgated at court and throughout the provinces to furnish standards for countless ages. Of these, the two matters of moral instruction and punishment bear most closely upon scholars and the people. The means by which the state molds its myriad subjects and nurtures its vital energies may also lie here. Were these measures the same as the institutions of successive ancient dynasties, or different? Or did they follow earlier precedents while modifying them? It is said that these two matters depend upon each other: is this indeed so? In their implementation down to the present, have there also been slight departures that ought to be corrected by restoring earlier practice? The instructions, proclamations, statutes, ordinances, and regulations are all extant, and you scholars have respectfully observed them for years. Moreover, our sagely Son of Heaven’s intention to honor moral instruction and exercise caution and compassion in punishment, repeatedly expressed in his edicts, has long been made known throughout the realm. Expound and celebrate these matters together, so that his plans and achievements may be made illustrious for all time. If you cherish the sincerity of one who offers humble celery or the warmth of the sun, please also express your views, thereby helping to bring about a resurgence of sagely virtue.

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
光氏盖其忠愛出於天性而學問才力
足以濟之故立朝大節燁然有非諸人
所可及者嘗觀其在哲宗時編進稽古
錄一書晦菴朱子謂其願忠君父之心
更歴三朝然後成就可備講筵進讀今
考其書有歴年圖有百官表有補圖表
之所未及上下數千百年治亂興衰之
迹無不備具至其序論有曰人君之道

punctuated: 光氏，盖其忠愛出於天性，而學問才力足以濟之，故立朝大節燁然，有非諸人所可及者。嘗觀其在哲宗時編進《稽古錄》一書，晦菴朱子謂其願忠君父之心，更歴三朝然後成就，可備講筵進讀。今考其書，有歴年圖，有百官表，有補圖表之所未及，上下數千百年治亂興衰之迹，無不備具。至其序論有曰：「人君之道一，其德三，其才五。有國家者，雖變化萬端，皆不外是。」朱子謂此尤為懇切，不可不使聖主聞之。夫朱子大儒，不阿所好，乃景慕思惟，汲汲欲以奏進，誠見此書之法戒昭然，有裨觀覽焉耳。肆我皇上正位以来，垂拱勵精，其要道至德，與夫中興之才，善美極盡，不可尚已。臣子無已之心，不識三事之中，有可敷揚以仰裨萬一者乎？抑果可以進讀經筵，如朱子之意否乎？諸士固多聞有得者
translation_en:
…Guang, whose loyalty and devotion surely sprang from his nature, while his learning and ability were sufficient to give them effect. Thus the outstanding integrity he displayed at court shone brilliantly, in ways beyond the reach of the others. I have examined the Record of Investigations into Antiquity (Jigu lu), which he compiled and presented during the reign of Zhezong. Master Zhu Xi, known as Hui’an, said that his desire to be loyal to his ruler and father had taken three reigns to reach fruition in this work, which could serve for reading before the emperor at court lectures. Examining the book now, we find chronological charts, tables of the various officials, and material supplementing what the charts and tables leave uncovered. It comprehensively records the course of order and disorder, flourishing and decline, over thousands of years. Its introductory discussion states: “The ruler’s Way is one; his virtues are three; his abilities are five. Although the circumstances confronting those who govern a state vary in myriad ways, none falls outside these.” Master Zhu said that this passage was especially earnest and pertinent, and that the sagely ruler must be made to hear it.

Master Zhu was a great Confucian scholar who did not flatter even those he admired. Yet he revered and pondered this work, eagerly wishing to present it to the throne. This was surely because he recognized that its models and warnings were clearly set forth and would benefit the emperor’s reading. Since Our Emperor assumed his rightful position, he has governed with effortless composure while devoting himself energetically to good government. His essential Way and consummate virtue, together with his abilities in bringing about a restoration, have attained the utmost goodness and excellence and cannot be surpassed. Yet the devotion of his servants knows no end: might there be something among these three matters that could be expounded to offer even the slightest assistance to His Majesty? And could this work indeed be read before him at the Classics Colloquium, as Master Zhu intended? You scholars are surely men of extensive learning and insight…

史外史御史又曰師氏保氏司諫禮曰

而有守人盡言而無諱其何道以致之

也，願悉言之，毋讓。

問：古者史不易職，諫不名官，昔人有是言矣。及觀《周禮》六官之屬，曰大史、小史、内史、外史、御史，又曰師氏、保氏、司諫。《禮》曰左右史，皆何所職，而名若是紛紛也？自漢唐而下，以及我國朝之盛，其沿革輕重之詳，可悉舉而言歟？夫是二者，在上長養而優容之爾，故歐陽修、吕公著、蘇軾、吕祖謙皆懇懇以為言。其說信乎否歟？或謂史須三長，擇言官以三事為先，又謂直筆不專於文學，威望不專於彈劾者，何歟？兹欲史盡職而有守，人盡言而無諱，其何道以致之？

問：治天下者審所尚。夏尚忠，商尚質，周尚文，信斯言也，其何所於始乎？夫文之與質，類也；忠、質則何以辨？先儒有謂忠則渾然誠確，無質可言，其說然歟？又有言商尚敬者，敬之與質又何以辨？商之所
translation_en:
… We hope you will explain everything fully, without holding back.

Question: It was said by men of old that in antiquity historians did not change their duties, and remonstrance was not the designation of an office. Yet among the offices subordinate to the six ministries in the Rites of Zhou, we find the Grand Scribe, Junior Scribe, Interior Scribe, Exterior Scribe, and Attendant Scribe, as well as the Mentor, Protector, and Remonstrator. The Book of Rites speaks of historians of the left and right. What were the duties of each, and why was there such a profusion of titles? From the Han and Tang onward, down to the flourishing age of our own dynasty, can you enumerate and explain in detail how these offices changed and how their relative importance varied? These two kinds of officials require those above them to nurture them and treat them with generous tolerance. Thus Ouyang Xiu, Lü Gongzhu, Su Shi, and Lü Zuqian all spoke earnestly on this matter. Are their arguments sound or not? Some say that a historian needs three strengths, and that three considerations should take priority in selecting remonstrance officials. Others say that forthright historical writing does not depend solely on literary learning, and that authority and prestige do not depend solely on impeachment. What do these statements mean? If we now wish historians to fulfill their duties and maintain their principles, and people to speak fully without concealment, by what means can this be achieved?

text:
何也史稱人庶繁殷府庫充斥豈類皆
虛語歟抑别有其說也仰惟我
皇上恤民重農超越前代遠甚歲一告饑發金
內帑大弛逋負而議者憂非可繼至建儲粟
以督吏治而民又患之未幾報罷茲欲
國裕而民康公私不至於偏病若之何
其可也請著于篇以觀憂國之論

punctuated: 何也？史稱人庶繁殷，府庫充斥，豈類皆虛語歟？抑别有其說也？仰惟我皇上恤民重農，超越前代遠甚。歲一告饑，發金內帑，大弛逋負，而議者憂非可繼。至建儲粟以督吏治，而民又患之，未幾報罷。茲欲國裕而民康，公私不至於偏病，若之何其可也？請著于篇，以觀憂國之論。
translation_en:
…why is this so? The histories state that the populace was numerous and prosperous and that the treasuries and storehouses were full. Could all such statements be empty words? Or is there another explanation?
Looking up respectfully to our Emperor, we reflect that his compassion for the people and emphasis on agriculture far surpass those of previous dynasties. Whenever famine is reported in a year, he disburses funds from the privy treasury and greatly remits outstanding obligations. Yet commentators worry that this cannot be sustained. When grain reserves were instituted as a means of holding officials accountable for their administration, the people also found this burdensome, and before long the measure was reportedly abolished. Now, if we wish the state to have ample resources and the people to live in well-being, with neither public nor private interests bearing a disproportionate burden, how can this be achieved? Please set out your views in writing, so that we may examine your arguments expressing concern for the state.

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

子曰：「大哉，堯之為君也！巍巍乎！唯天為大，唯堯則之。蕩蕩乎！民無能名焉。巍巍乎其有成功也！煥乎其有文章！」

左鎰

同考試官主事李批：「堯之有可見者，止於成功文章，正見其德之大不可名處。此作能發明之，末復推言性道，人皆可為，是可以訓矣。錄之。」

同考試官署郎中高批：「純明雅正，為文之式。」

同考試官都給事中蔡批：「堯德難名，正其所以配天處，而唯此可見，益見其所以難名。此作能發之，宜錄以為式。」

同考試官修撰倫批：「堯之德，吾夫子之言，皆學者難容筆處。此作摹寫曲盡，結推本率性上，尤為根極之論。」

考試官學士郭批：「說堯德之盛處最是。」

考試官學士張批：「得聖人賛堯語意。」
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: “Great indeed was Yao as a ruler! How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone took it as his model. How boundless! The people could find no words to name it. How lofty were his accomplishments! How brilliant were his cultural achievements!”

Zuo Yi

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, a Secretary: “What can be perceived of Yao is confined to his accomplishments and cultural achievements. This reveals precisely where the greatness of his virtue surpasses description. This essay succeeds in elucidating this point. At the end, it further develops the discussion of human nature and the Way, explaining that everyone can attain this. It can thus serve as instruction. Include it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, an Acting Director: “Pure, lucid, refined, and correct: a model for composition.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Cai, a Chief Supervising Secretary: “The indescribability of Yao’s virtue is precisely what makes it match Heaven. That only these achievements can be perceived makes still clearer why his virtue is so difficult to describe. This essay succeeds in elucidating this point and should be included as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lun, a Compiler: “Both Yao’s virtue and the words of our Master are matters on which students find it difficult to add anything in writing. This essay portrays them exhaustively in all their subtleties. Its conclusion traces their foundation to following one’s nature: an especially penetrating discussion of the ultimate root.”

Comment by Examiner Guo, an Academician: “The passage explaining the fullness of Yao’s virtue is particularly apt.”

Comment by Examiner Zhang, an Academician: “It captures the meaning of the sage’s words in praise of Yao.”

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
聖人賛帝德之大不可名而有可見者焉盖帝
堯之德配天而難名其可見者功業文章耳宜
孔子之極賛其大也歟其意盖謂稟聖德而首
出庶物膺天命而奄有四海大矣哉帝堯之為
君乎何以言之盖物莫不有高者而天無不覆
其孰尚之亦莫不有大者而天無不包其孰過
之巍巍高大曰唯天爾唯堯則之而不可以天
人殊觀也故生斯世者為斯民者以耕以鑿忘
帝力於何有固無得而稱焉相生相養順帝則
===
於不知將何以為頌焉蕩蕩廣遠至德難名亦
如天之不可以言語形容也夫雖不可名然亦
豈無可見者乎自今觀之光被四表格于上下
功業之成巍巍乎其高大如百姓則昭明也萬
邦則協和也治若此其盛而况其德之不顯者
邪禮樂宣著法度昭章文章之盛煥乎其光明
如羲和命而嵗時叙虞舜舉而政教敷功由是
以成而况其德之難言者邪夫於天於堯皆曰
唯見其脗合而無間爾於成功文章皆曰有見

punctuated: 聖人賛帝德之大不可名，而有可見者焉。盖帝堯之德配天而難名，其可見者功業文章耳，宜孔子之極賛其大也歟！其意盖謂：稟聖德而首出庶物，膺天命而奄有四海，大矣哉，帝堯之為君乎！何以言之？盖物莫不有高者，而天無不覆，其孰尚之？亦莫不有大者，而天無不包，其孰過之？巍巍高大，曰唯天爾，唯堯則之，而不可以天人殊觀也。故生斯世者，為斯民者，以耕以鑿，忘帝力於何有，固無得而稱焉；相生相養，順帝則於不知，將何以為頌焉？蕩蕩廣遠，至德難名，亦如天之不可以言語形容也。夫雖不可名，然亦豈無可見者乎？自今觀之，光被四表，格于上下，功業之成，巍巍乎其高大。如百姓則昭明也，萬邦則協和也。治若此其盛，而况其德之不顯者邪！禮樂宣著，法度昭章，文章之盛，煥乎其光明。如羲和命而嵗時叙，虞舜舉而政教敷。功由是以成，而况其德之難言者邪！夫於天於堯皆曰「唯」，見其脗合而無間爾；於成功文章皆曰「有」，見
translation_en:
The Sage praised the greatness of the emperor’s virtue: it could not be named, yet there were aspects of it that could be seen. Emperor Yao’s virtue matched Heaven and was difficult to name; what could be seen were simply his achievements and cultural accomplishments. How fitting that Confucius should praise his greatness to the utmost! His meaning was this: endowed with sagely virtue, Yao stood foremost among all beings; receiving Heaven’s mandate, he possessed all within the Four Seas. Great indeed was Emperor Yao as a ruler! How may this be explained? Among things there are those that are lofty, yet Heaven covers everything: what could rise above it? There are likewise those that are great, yet Heaven embraces everything: what could surpass it? Towering in height and greatness—this is said of Heaven alone. Yao alone took it as his model, so Heaven and the human ruler cannot be regarded as separate. Thus those born into that age, those who were his people, ploughed their fields and dug their wells, oblivious to what the emperor’s power contributed to them; they could find nothing to name in praise. They sustained and nourished one another, following the emperor’s standards without knowing it: how, then, could they compose a eulogy? Vast and far-reaching, his supreme virtue was difficult to name, just as Heaven cannot be described in words.

Yet although it could not be named, could there really have been nothing visible? Looking back from the present, his radiance reached the four extremities and extended above and below. His completed achievements towered in their height and greatness. The hundred families were enlightened, and the myriad states were brought into harmony. His government flourished to such a degree—how much more, then, the virtue that remained unseen! Ritual and music were manifest, laws and standards clearly displayed; his cultural accomplishments shone brilliantly. Xi and He were appointed, and the year and seasons were set in order; Yu Shun was raised to office, and government and moral instruction spread abroad. Through these his achievements were completed—how much more, then, the virtue that was difficult to express! In speaking of both Heaven and Yao, Confucius used the word “alone,” showing their perfect correspondence without any gap between them; in speaking of completed achievements and cultural accomplishments, he used “there were,” showing …

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
其無能名者有此爾惟不可名斯其所以配天
也惟是可見斯其所以難名也則堯為君之大
不亦章章明甚矣乎抑記傳所載聖賢所稱多
並舉唐虞而此獨賛堯之大何歟盖舉舜側微
而授之天下紹其後以成無為之治固堯之為
之也觀書稱欽明文思安安允恭克讓其相授
受曰執中無亦率性而已其謂不可名者豈信
有不可及者哉故曰人皆可以為堯舜
行而世為天下法言而世為天下則
===

自是大家數文字錄以為式夫誰曰不宜
同考試官給事中葉 批 自古王者制作皆是天
理運用故自盡善此作獨能究極是必知王道者
同考試官編修程 批 爾雅渾厚亦可以為法
則矣
同考試官編修張 批 莊重典雅能言制作之
精蘊可式

punctuated:
其無能名者有此爾。惟不可名，斯其所以配天也；惟是可見，斯其所以難名也。則堯為君之大，不亦章章明甚矣乎？抑記傳所載、聖賢所稱，多並舉唐虞，而此獨賛堯之大，何歟？盖舉舜側微而授之天下，紹其後以成無為之治，固堯之為之也。觀《書》稱「欽明文思安安，允恭克讓」，其相授受曰「執中」，無亦率性而已。其謂不可名者，豈信有不可及者哉？故曰：「人皆可以為堯舜。」

行而世為天下法，言而世為天下則。

同考試官主事林批：春容雅澹，而規度整然，自是大家數文字，錄以為式，夫誰曰不宜？

同考試官給事中葉批：自古王者制作，皆是天理運用，故自盡善。此作獨能究極，是必知王道者。

同考試官編修程批：爾雅渾厚，亦可以為法則矣。

同考試官編修張批：莊重典雅，能言制作之精蘊，可式。
translation_en:
…that what could not be named had these manifestations. Precisely because it could not be named, he could match Heaven; precisely because these manifestations could be seen, his greatness was difficult to name. Is not Yao’s greatness as a ruler thus abundantly clear? Yet the historical records and the praises of sages and worthies generally mention Tang and Yu together. Why does this passage praise Yao’s greatness alone? It was surely Yao who raised Shun from humble obscurity and entrusted All-under-Heaven to him, allowing him to succeed and complete a government through nonaction. Consider how the Book of Documents describes Yao as “reverent, discerning, accomplished, and thoughtful, naturally at ease,” and Shun as “truly reverent and capable of yielding.” In transmitting rule from one to the other, the instruction was to “hold fast to the mean.” Was this not simply following their inherent nature? Could what is called impossible to name really be beyond anyone’s reach? Thus it is said: “Everyone can become a Yao or a Shun.”

His actions serve for generations as a model for All-under-Heaven; his words serve for generations as a standard for All-under-Heaven.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Bureau Secretary: Graceful, composed, elegant, and restrained, with thoroughly orderly structure and measure: this is certainly writing of a great master’s caliber. Who could say it is inappropriate to record it as a model?

Comment by Associate Examiner Ye, Supervising Secretary: Since antiquity, the institutions and ordinances established by true kings have all been the workings of heavenly principle, and hence have naturally attained perfect goodness. This essay alone fathoms the matter fully; its author must understand the kingly Way.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cheng, Hanlin Compiler: Refined and substantial, this too can serve as a model and standard.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Hanlin Junior Compiler: Dignified, classical, and elegant, it articulates the essential profundities of establishing institutions and ordinances. It may serve as a model.

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
考試官學士郭批體認言行意親切且不苟
下一語非精於理不能也
考試官學士張批斂華就實是說理文字
中庸言君子制作出於已而垂憲於人者遠也
甚矣制作之難也觀君子之行與言而天下後
世法則之非其至善能然乎中庸謂王天下有
三重至此以為君子者德位兼於身信從徵於
民盖凡議禮制度考文動無不宜而于天人上
下道無不合故自其心術之微而達諸經綸之
===
妙或立綱而陳紀或開物以成務凡顯設於朝
廷而敷布於天下者固以定一代之章程爾未
始必於傳遠也而何以世世法焉盖世雖不同
而所同者理君子有行既不出乎民生日用之
外而允協乎天道人心之公則後有作者皆率
之為成憲如禮也度也文也亦惟以其行之於
千百世之上者而持守於千百世之下矣又自
夫謀慮之懿而著為訓典之常或以載諸簡冊
或以誥之臣民凡發揮於文辭而傳播於天下

三重至此以為君子者德位兼於身信從徵於
民盖凡議禮制度考文動無不宜而于天人上
下道無不合故自其心術之微而達諸經綸之
===
妙或立綱而陳紀或開物以成務凡顯設於朝
廷而敷布於天下者固以定一代之章程爾未
始必於傳遠也而何以世世法焉盖世雖不同
而所同者理君子有行既不出乎民生日用之
外而允協乎天道人心之公則後有作者皆率
之為成憲如禮也度也文也亦惟以其行之於
千百世之上者而持守於千百世之下矣又自
夫謀慮之懿而著為訓典之常或以載諸簡冊
或以誥之臣民凡發揮於文辭而傳播於天下
punctuated:
考試官學士郭批：體認言行意親切，且不苟下一語，非精於理不能也。

考試官學士張批：斂華就實，是說理文字。

中庸言君子制作出於已而垂憲於人者遠也。

甚矣，制作之難也！觀君子之行與言，而天下後世法則之，非其至善能然乎？中庸謂王天下有三重，至此以為君子者，德位兼於身，信從徵於民。盖凡議禮、制度、考文，動無不宜，而于天人上下，道無不合。故自其心術之微而達諸經綸之妙，或立綱而陳紀，或開物以成務，凡顯設於朝廷而敷布於天下者，固以定一代之章程爾，未始必於傳遠也。而何以世世法焉？盖世雖不同，而所同者理。君子有行，既不出乎民生日用之外，而允協乎天道人心之公，則後有作者，皆率之為成憲。如禮也、度也、文也，亦惟以其行之於千百世之上者，而持守於千百世之下矣。又自夫謀慮之懿而著為訓典之常，或以載諸簡冊，或以誥之臣民，凡發揮於文辭而傳播於天下
translation_en:
Examiner, Academician Guo, comments: The writer grasps intimately the meaning of words and conduct, and does not set down a single word carelessly. Without a refined understanding of principle, this would be impossible.

Examiner, Academician Zhang, comments: Restraining ornament and attending to substance, this is writing that elucidates principle.

The Doctrine of the Mean says that the gentleman’s institutions originate in himself and endure far into the future as standards for others.

How difficult it is to establish institutions! When we observe the gentleman’s conduct and words, and see that all under Heaven and later generations take them as models and standards, could this happen unless they were supremely good? The Doctrine of the Mean speaks of three weighty responsibilities in ruling all under Heaven. At this point, the gentleman it describes possesses both virtue and position, and the people’s trust and obedience bear witness to him. In deliberating on ritual, establishing regulations, and examining written forms, his every action is fitting; his Way accords in every respect with Heaven and humanity, above and below. Thus, from the subtleties of his inner disposition he proceeds to the wonders of ordering the world: he may establish guiding principles and set out rules, or open up an understanding of things and bring undertakings to completion. Everything publicly instituted at court and promulgated throughout the realm serves, to be sure, to settle the statutes and regulations of a single age; it need not have been intended for transmission into the distant future. Why, then, do successive generations take it as their model? Though ages differ, the principle they share is the same. The gentleman’s conduct does not extend beyond the people’s everyday life and needs, yet it fully accords with the impartiality of Heaven’s Way and the human heart. Consequently, those who later establish institutions all follow it as settled precedent. Whether ritual, regulations, or written forms, they simply uphold, thousands and hundreds of generations later, what he put into practice thousands and hundreds of generations earlier. Again, the excellence of his deliberations finds expression in enduring teachings and canons, whether recorded in books or proclaimed to officials and people. Everything expounded in literary expression and disseminated throughout the realm …

translation_en:
…were intended merely to set forth the grand counsels of a single age, with no initial intention of transmitting them far into the future. Why, then, do successive generations take them as their standard? Though people differ, the heart they share is the same. The gentleman’s words arise from his own practice and inward understanding and express the correct principles governing human relationships and all things. Those who subsequently transmit his teachings therefore necessarily follow them as established precedents. What he deliberated upon, instituted, and examined likewise consists of words spoken hundreds or thousands of generations earlier, from which people hundreds or thousands of generations later take their standard of correctness. Ah! How magnificent are the gentleman’s institutions! And could such a man fail to have few faults?

Consider how Huangdi, Yao, and Shun let their robes hang down, and the world was well governed. What is recorded in the Book of Changes and the Book of Documents can still be examined today, and no one has been able to alter it. But when evidence concerning Xia and Shang was lacking, and Confucius held no official position, what could even he do? Thus he said, “I follow Zhou.” Nevertheless, only after possessing Heaven’s virtue can one speak of the kingly Way; only after hearing teachings on human nature and the Way of Heaven can one institute rites and create music. This is indeed the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean when it speaks of the human Way and of occupying a high position without arrogance.

“Attend carefully to instruction in the schools, reinforcing it with the duties of filial devotion and respect for elder brothers.”
By Lin Chun.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Secretary: Precise and incisive, elegant and vigorous. Expositions of the meaning of Mencius written like this are exceedingly rare. Include it as a model for those who indulge in empty rhetoric.

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Supervising Secretary: It profoundly grasps the intent of Mencius’s advice to King Hui. It should be included as a model.

To attend carefully to the task of educating the people and give weight to the foundation of the human Way is to bring the Kingly Way to fulfillment. Education and moral transformation are pressing duties of the state, while filial piety and fraternal respect are the foundation of the human Way. Is this not what kingly government attends to carefully and especially esteems? When Mencius once explained the Kingly Way to King Hui of Liang, this passage addressed educating the people after making them prosperous. His meaning was that, in the flourishing days of Yin and Zhou, each neighborhood had a xiang school and each district a xu school, so that everyone studied. The xiang schools taught ritual propriety, and the xu schools assessed virtue; moral transformation was thus fully achieved. Yet this Way has long gone unpracticed. If one wishes to institute kingly government, can one fail to attend carefully to this? One must give it comprehensive, detailed, and scrupulous consideration: bring teachers and scholars together to undertake the work, gather pupils and show them the proper direction, and supervise and admonish them in due measure, so that all who attend school cease clinging to their old habits. title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
為學者皆不怠於所有事焉夫教以明倫也而
親長為人倫之至重學以致道也而孝悌實人
道之所先斯義之不明也久矣欲興教化可不
申重於此乎必也致丁寧反覆之意以立愛惟
親而仁之實在是子之事親當隨其所在而致
隆於常於變而自得其宜之為順也立敬惟長
而義之實在是弟之事兄當隨其所值以伸情
於小於大而各得其當之為安也若然則教法
已定而不紊先後有序而可循孝悌之道自行
===
於家邦而仁讓之化可達於四海矣王道不亦
大成乎抑斯道也其來尚矣堯之時水土初平
稷降種而烝民乃粒契典教而四方風動此治
化之極而三代之隆皆以此也周衰而王政熄
故孟子於齊梁之君有望焉而竟不一遇豈天
未欲平治天下哉然百世之下有能因其說而
行之則唐虞之化可幾矣於乎此有天下者之
所宜致思也
易

為學者皆不怠於所有事焉。夫教以明倫也，而親長為人倫之至重；學以致道也，而孝悌實人道之所先。斯義之不明也久矣，欲興教化，可不申重於此乎？必也致丁寧反覆之意，以立愛惟親，而仁之實在是，子之事親當隨其所在而致隆於常於變，而自得其宜之為順也；立敬惟長，而義之實在是，弟之事兄當隨其所值以伸情於小於大，而各得其當之為安也。若然，則教法已定而不紊，先後有序而可循，孝悌之道自行於家邦，而仁讓之化可達於四海矣。王道不亦大成乎？抑斯道也，其來尚矣。堯之時，水土初平，稷降種而烝民乃粒，契典教而四方風動。此治化之極，而三代之隆皆以此也。周衰而王政熄，故孟子於齊梁之君有望焉，而竟不一遇，豈天未欲平治天下哉？然百世之下，有能因其說而行之，則唐虞之化可幾矣。於乎！此有天下者之所宜致思也。

易
translation_en:
…so that all who pursue learning remain diligent in their duties. Teaching serves to clarify human relationships, among which those with parents and elders are of the greatest importance; learning serves to realize the Way, and filial devotion and respect for elder brothers are indeed foremost in the human Way. This principle has long remained obscure. If one wishes to promote moral instruction, can one fail to emphasize it repeatedly? One must offer earnest and repeated admonitions: love is established through one’s parents, and herein lies the substance of benevolence. In serving their parents, sons should give the fullest expression to their devotion in whatever circumstances they find themselves, both ordinary and exceptional, naturally attaining the fitting conduct that constitutes filial compliance. Respect is established through one’s elders, and herein lies the substance of righteousness. In serving their elder brothers, younger brothers should express their affection in whatever situations they encounter, in matters small and great, attaining in each case the appropriate conduct that brings harmony. If this is done, the methods of instruction will be established without disorder, and their sequence will provide an orderly course to follow. The Way of filial devotion and fraternal respect will then prevail naturally in families and states, and the transforming influence of benevolence and deference can reach all within the Four Seas. Would not the Kingly Way thereby be brought to full fruition?

Indeed, this Way has a long history. In Yao’s time, when the waters and lands had only just been brought under control, Ji bestowed seeds, and the multitude came to eat grain; Xie took charge of instruction, and all four quarters responded as grass bends before the wind. This was the highest achievement of orderly government and moral transformation, and the flourishing of the Three Dynasties depended entirely upon it. When the Zhou declined, kingly government died out. Thus Mengzi placed his hopes in the rulers of Qi and Liang, yet ultimately met with no ruler who would put his teachings into practice. Could it be that Heaven did not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world? Nevertheless, even a hundred generations later, if someone can act upon his teachings, the transforming influence of the ages of Tang and Yu—that is, Yao and Shun—may be approached. Ah! This is what those who rule All under Heaven ought to ponder.

Book of Changes

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
權綱獨運文理密察之懿周庶事而心體常明
所以治有者不既立其本矣乎治莫大乎法天
亦莫大乎因時大有之君道與天而同運政與
時而偕行憲天之聰明以臨民而動合乎時中
之用順天之休命以敷乂而事從乎時措之宜
所以治有者不既妙其用矣乎以是而位乎天
德也德惟善政可以任輔相裁成之責以是而
奉乎天時也時惟建事可以成彌綸參贊之能
仁義中正舉一世而甄陶德教之洋溢蓋有化
===
行於無外者矣禮樂刑政達四海而不悖耿光
之衣被蓋有垂裕於無疆者矣占之所以為元
亨者如此是知富有天下未足以為大有備衆
善以致元亨其斯以為大有乎雖然君德莫先
乎剛健矣而六五固柔中之主也其為大有何
也夫子序卦曰有大者不可以盈卦以柔中為
主意取諸此乎而占之致亨則固剛健為之本
也周公繫爻曰厥孚交如威如吉其義備矣
顯道神德行是故可與酬酢可與祐神矣

之衣被蓋有垂裕於無疆者矣占之所以為元

也周公繫爻曰厥孚交如威如吉其義備矣
顯道神德行是故可與酬酢可與祐神矣
punctuated:
權綱獨運，文理密察之懿，周庶事而心體常明，所以治有者，不既立其本矣乎？治莫大乎法天，亦莫大乎因時。大有之君，道與天而同運，政與時而偕行，憲天之聰明以臨民，而動合乎時中之用；順天之休命以敷乂，而事從乎時措之宜。所以治有者，不既妙其用矣乎？以是而位乎天德也，德惟善政，可以任輔相裁成之責；以是而奉乎天時也，時惟建事，可以成彌綸參贊之能。仁義中正，舉一世而甄陶，德教之洋溢，蓋有化行於無外者矣；禮樂刑政，達四海而不悖，耿光之衣被，蓋有垂裕於無疆者矣。占之所以為元亨者如此。是知富有天下，未足以為大有；備衆善以致元亨，其斯以為大有乎？雖然，君德莫先乎剛健矣，而六五固柔中之主也，其為大有何也？夫子《序卦》曰：「有大者不可以盈。」卦以柔中為主，意取諸此乎？而占之致亨，則固剛健為之本也。周公繫爻曰：「厥孚交如，威如，吉。」其義備矣。
顯道神德行，是故可與酬酢，可與祐神矣。
translation_en:
…he alone wields the guiding authority. With the excellence of his refined discernment and close scrutiny, he attends to all affairs while the substance of his mind remains ever clear. Has he not thereby established the foundation for governing what he possesses? In government nothing is greater than modeling oneself on Heaven, and nothing is greater than responding to the times. The ruler of Great Possession moves in the Way together with Heaven, and his government proceeds in step with the times. He models himself on Heaven’s perceptiveness and understanding in presiding over the people, so that his actions accord with what is fitting at each moment; he follows Heaven’s gracious mandate in extending good order, so that his undertakings suit the circumstances of their enactment. Has he not thereby perfected the practical application of governing what he possesses? By this he takes his place in Heaven’s virtue: virtue consists in good government, enabling him to assume responsibility for assisting, regulating, and completing Heaven’s work. By this he serves Heaven’s seasons: the seasons provide for the establishment of undertakings, enabling him to encompass all things and participate in and assist their transformation. Through benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and rectitude, he molds the whole age. His moral instruction overflows, bringing transformation everywhere, with nothing beyond its reach. Rites, music, punishments, and government extend throughout the Four Seas without discord. His radiant light clothes all, bequeathing blessings without limit. Such is the reason that the divination promises supreme success. We thus know that possessing all the wealth under Heaven does not suffice to constitute Great Possession. Is it not the completeness of all virtues, bringing supreme success, that constitutes Great Possession? Nevertheless, no ruler’s virtue takes precedence over strength and vigor, yet the six in the fifth place is a yielding ruler occupying the central position. How, then, does this constitute Great Possession? The Master says in the Sequence of the Hexagrams: “One whose possessions are great must not become full of pride.” Is this the idea behind the hexagram’s taking a yielding, central line as its ruler? Yet strength and vigor are indeed the foundation for attaining the success foretold by the divination. The Duke of Zhou appended this statement to the line: “His sincerity evokes a response; with an imposing bearing, good fortune.” The meaning is fully expressed therein.
It makes the Way manifest and renders virtuous conduct numinous; thus it may be used to respond to things and to assist the spirits.

Cheng Xiumin

Associate Examiner Li, Secretary, comments: “He expounds the functions of the milfoil stalks and hexagrams, leaving almost no hidden meaning unexplored. One may indeed discuss the Book of Changes with him.”

Associate Examiner Gao, Acting Director, comments: “For students of the Book of Changes, taking this as their model will suffice.”

Associate Examiner Cai, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “Writers generally can explain how the Way is made manifest through the statements and how conduct is rendered numinous through the numbers. Its author must have a profound understanding of the Book of Changes.”

The Great Commentary traces the wondrous efficacy of the Book of Changes, which affords assistance to spirits and humans. The function of the milfoil stalks and hexagrams lies in the wondrous interplay of the subtle and the manifest. There is thus good reason why they can respond to inquiries and assist the spirits! Now, in the method of manipulating milfoil stalks to obtain a hexagram, manipulating the stalks produces numbers, and the completed hexagram has its statements. Statements and numbers are the principal elements of the Book of Changes. All the principles of good fortune, misfortune, regret, and humiliation are aspects of the Way concealed in the most subtle realm; the statements make them manifest. When one consults the Changes [?], it provides an answer. Illuminating what has passed and discerning what is to come, it knows all things, whether distant or near, obscure or profound; probing complexities and seeking out what is hidden, it fully investigates the beginnings of gain and loss, anxiety and apprehension. title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
與之俱顯乎人事云為之迹德行之日可見者
也而數實神之揲筮而有所值焉鼓羣動於趨
避之途而變通以盡利泯機緘於應迹之外而
神化以宜民德行囿於數其不因之以神乎蓍
卦之妙如是是以寂感莫測其方而幽明兼效
其用彼吉凶之變凡民不能以前知惟夫考之
辭與數也受命如嚮而天下得以通其志示民
無隱而百姓得以與其能與之酬酢可以汎應
而無窮矣吉凶之故鬼神不能以告人惟夫求
===
之數與辭也成能乎天地而啟造化不言之機
幽賛於神明而前斯民未有之用與之祐神可
以感通而無間矣是則蓍卦之用出入乎微顯
之間而貫通乎幽明之際易為天地鬼神之奧
詎不信哉雖然道與德行非二物也德行之神
即所謂道道之顯即所謂德行形而上下者也
此所以能酬酢祐神通幽明之故而天人合一
者也程子曰體用一源顯微無間張子曰一故
神兩故化其諸有得於此乎

之數與辭也成能乎天地而啓造化不言之機
幽贊於神明而前斯民未有之用與之祐神可
以感通而無間矣是則蓍卦之用出入乎微顯
之間而貫通乎幽明之際易爲天地鬼神之輿
詎不信哉雖然道與德行非二物也德行之神
即所謂道道之顯即所謂德行形而上下皆也
此所以能酬酢祐神通幽明之故而天人合一
者也程子曰體用一源顯微無間張子曰一故
神兩故化其諸有得於此乎
punctuated: 與之俱顯乎？人事云為之迹，德行之日可見者也，而數實神之。揲筮而有所值焉，鼓羣動於趨避之途，而變通以盡利；泯機緘於應迹之外，而神化以宜民。德行囿於數，其不因之以神乎？蓍卦之妙如是，是以寂感莫測其方，而幽明兼效其用。彼吉凶之變，凡民不能以前知，惟夫考之辭與數也，受命如嚮，而天下得以通其志；示民無隱，而百姓得以與其能。與之酬酢，可以汎應而無窮矣。吉凶之故，鬼神不能以告人，惟夫求之數與辭也，成能乎天地，而啟造化不言之機；幽賛於神明，而前斯民未有之用。與之祐神，可以感通而無間矣。是則蓍卦之用，出入乎微顯之間，而貫通乎幽明之際。《易》為天地鬼神之奧，詎不信哉？雖然，道與德行非二物也。德行之神，即所謂道；道之顯，即所謂德行，形而上下者也。此所以能酬酢祐神、通幽明之故，而天人合一者也。程子曰：「體用一源，顯微無間。」張子曰：「一故神，兩故化。」其諸有得於此乎？
translation_en:
…does it not become manifest together with them? The traces of what people say and do in human affairs are the daily visible manifestations of virtuous conduct; yet it is the numbers that render them numinous. When the milfoil stalks are manipulated in divination, a result is obtained. They stir all activity along the paths of seeking and avoiding, adapting to change so as to realize every benefit; they conceal their workings beyond the outward traces of response, bringing about numinous transformations that benefit the people. Virtuous conduct is encompassed within the numbers: does it not thereby become numinous? Such is the subtle efficacy of the milfoil and hexagrams. Thus, whether quiescent or responding, their manner of operation cannot be fathomed, and their efficacy extends to both the hidden and the manifest. Ordinary people cannot foreknow changes of good and ill fortune. Only by examining the statements and numbers can they do so: these receive an inquiry and respond like an echo, enabling all under Heaven to communicate their intentions; they disclose things to the people without concealment, enabling the common people to share in their capacity. Through reciprocal exchange with them, one can respond universally and without limit. Ghosts and spirits cannot tell people the causes of good and ill fortune. Only by seeking these in the numbers and statements can one fulfill the capacities of Heaven and Earth and disclose the unspoken workings of creation, secretly assist the spiritual powers, and open up uses hitherto unavailable to the people. Through them, one can assist the spirits and achieve sympathetic communication without interruption.

Thus the efficacy of the milfoil and hexagrams moves between the subtle and the manifest and penetrates the boundary between the hidden and the visible. Is it not indeed true that the Book of Changes is the repository of the mysteries of Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits? Nevertheless, the Way and virtuous conduct are not two separate things. The numinous aspect of virtuous conduct is what is called the Way; the manifestation of the Way is what is called virtuous conduct. These are what lies above and below physical form. This is why they can engage in reciprocal exchange, assist the spirits, and connect the hidden and the manifest: Heaven and humanity form a unity. Master Cheng said, “Substance and function have a single source; there is no separation between the manifest and the subtle.” Master Zhang said, “Because it is one, it is numinous; because it is two, it transforms.” Did they not perhaps grasp something of this?

之，則所以服大僚、宅百揆者，非其左右厥辟矣乎？惟茲鄰者，孰為之哉？命官分爵，莫親于臣，而鄰實繫之，則所以胥教誨、胥保惠者，固其前後有位者乎？因臣而思其職，為上為德，任何重也！舉職而加之臣，有馮有翼，責斯備也！帝之反覆於咏歎之間若此，則其警禹者至矣。
禹聞而即俞之，以為夫人莫不知有臣也，未知其切於鄰也；惟以鄰視臣，則有見於圖幾之不易矣。亦莫不知有鄰也，未知其賴於臣也；惟責臣以鄰，則有見於敬事之當先矣。予始發之而祗承乎帝，思效其恭也；帝復歎之而知臣為難，愈見其重也。是盖先得此心之所同然者矣，而臣何以圖稱也哉？
夫以帝曰吁，則信之既篤，而其樂善也誠；禹曰俞，則契之益深，而其責難也切。盛世君臣之相告戒，意氣之感也，有如是夫！《易》曰：「上下交而其志同也。」又曰：「同人于野，亨。」則聖人之貴同也尚矣。後世君臣想見唐虞之盛，孰不嘉樂，而顧每失之睽者何哉？求比於同，而非其志也。
translation_en:
…this role. Thus, is not the purpose of holding high office and presiding over the hundred affairs to assist one’s sovereign? And who are these close companions? Among those appointed to offices and invested with ranks, none are closer than the ministers; upon them, indeed, this companionship depends. Surely, then, those who instruct and admonish one another, protect and favor one another, are the officeholders attending the ruler before and behind? To think of ministers is to consider their duties: serving their sovereign and fostering his virtue—how weighty their charge! To lay these duties upon ministers, as those upon whom he relies and by whom he is supported, is to make their responsibility complete. Such was the Emperor’s repeated pondering and sighing: his admonition to Yu could go no further.
Hearing this, Yu immediately assented. He considered that everyone knew of ministers, but did not understand how intimately their role involved being close companions. Only by regarding ministers as close companions could one perceive the difficulty of attending to the first stirrings of events. Everyone likewise knew of close companions, but did not understand that this role depended upon ministers. Only by charging ministers to act as close companions could one perceive that reverent attention to affairs must come first. “When I first raised this matter and reverently addressed the Emperor, I sought to render my devoted service. Now that the Emperor has sighed over it in turn, recognizing the difficulty of being a minister, the gravity of that role becomes still clearer. He has already grasped what our hearts alike acknowledge. How, then, can I, his minister, contrive to fulfill it?”
When the Emperor said “Ah!”, his trust was already firm, and his delight in goodness sincere. When Yu said “Yes,” their mutual understanding grew still deeper, and his insistence upon the difficult demands of duty was earnest. Such was the mutual admonition of sovereign and minister in a flourishing age, and such their answering sympathy in spirit and purpose! The Book of Changes says: “Those above and those below interact, and their purposes are the same.” It also says: “Fellowship with others in the open country: success.” The sages’ esteem for unity is indeed of long standing. When rulers and ministers of later ages imagine the flourishing times of Tang and Yu—the ages of Yao and Shun—who does not admire and delight in them? Yet why do they so often go astray into discord? They seek affiliation through agreement, but not unity of purpose.

…how could such love ever have an end! For prolonging the dynasty’s allotted fortune rests with Heaven; securing Heaven’s Mandate rests with virtue. Why does the minister wish the king to employ virtue to win the allegiance of the regional lords and bring harmony to the misguided people? Simply because the regional lords are the state’s defenses, and the people its foundation. When the foundation is firm and the defenses established, people give their allegiance and Heaven draws near. Yet even if Zhou should fully match the years of Xia, the minister’s heart would not be satisfied; even if it should endure no less long than Yin, his heart would still not be satisfied. He wishes that, from now until ten thousand years hence, our Zhou alone may forever protect the people. Sons will succeed the king, and grandsons succeed the sons. Generation after generation, they will forever enjoy the blessings of the plans bequeathed to them and gloriously continue the succession to Heaven’s allotted rule, receiving the regional lords at court and caring for the myriad people, as constant through ten thousand years as through a single day. Forever inheriting the legacy of provision for their descendants, they will maintain unchanged [?] the government of a sovereign who faces the light, benefiting the central lands and thereby bringing peace to the four quarters, never declining however distant the future. Above, they will preserve their forebears’ blessings and extend the dynasty’s fortune and succession without limit; below, they will secure the people’s livelihood and transmit blessings and bounty without end. Only when this is achieved will August Heaven’s trust not have been in vain; only then can the former kings rejoice in their reception of the Mandate, and the minister’s hopes will likewise be fulfilled. How, then, could our king fail diligently to exercise luminous virtue, making it the foundation for firmly securing Heaven’s Mandate?

He said, “Employ virtue to pray to Heaven,” and “Through the common people, receive Heaven’s enduring Mandate.” For Heaven protects the people below and establishes rulers for them. title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
於後者不其大歟此宮室既成而燕飲以落之
其頌禱之詞盖謂吾王之夢卜協吉男子乃生
凡吾祝願於今重有期望於後也豈但衣之裳
弄之璋而已哉皆將備章服之榮昭物采之辨
純朱之芾本宗服之垂以蔽膝而禮秩尊矣衮
衣之下望之皇如也黃朱之芾支庶服之繫以
在股而等威定矣繡裳之上映之煥如也夫然
則主器正而元良之有託公族衍而名分之素
明後嗣之美何如哉由是服以稱其位焉位以
===
别其居焉支也膺茅土之錫立一國之室家而
為君固將資其藩垣屏翰之力乎本也撫方夏
之大保天下之室家而為王固將以為天地神
人之主乎夫然則不戢不那而百辟之為憲之
綱之紀而萬民之攸𡉏後嗣之盛何如哉吁此
吾王之所甚願而臣下之所拳拳者茲室也固
永為後世之那居也與吾於是而知詩人之善
頌禱矣愛其君而及其嗣且先之以弄璋云者
致尚德之意也盖德粹而後嗣賢嗣賢而後室

則主器正而元良之有託公族衍而名分之素
明後嗣之美何如哉由是服以稱其位焉位以
===
別其居焉支也膺茅土之錫立一國之室家而
爲君固將資其藩垣屏翰之力乎本也撫方夏
之大保天下之室家而爲王固將以爲天地神
人之主乎夫然則不戢不那而百辟之爲憲之
綱之紀而萬民之攸塈後嗣之盛何如哉吁此
吾王之所甚願而臣下之所拳拳者茲室也固
永爲後世之那居也與吾於是而知詩人之善
頌禱矣愛其君而及其嗣且先之以弄璋云者
啟尚德之意也蓋德粹而後嗣賢嗣賢而後室
punctuated: 於後者，不其大歟？此宮室既成，而燕飲以落之，其頌禱之詞，盖謂吾王之夢卜協吉，男子乃生。凡吾祝願於今，重有期望於後也，豈但衣之裳、弄之璋而已哉？皆將備章服之榮，昭物采之辨。純朱之芾，本宗服之，垂以蔽膝，而禮秩尊矣；衮衣之下，望之皇如也。黃朱之芾，支庶服之，繫以在股，而等威定矣；繡裳之上，映之煥如也。夫然，則主器正而元良之有託，公族衍而名分之素明，後嗣之美何如哉？由是，服以稱其位焉，位以别其居焉。支也，膺茅土之錫，立一國之室家而為君，固將資其藩垣屏翰之力乎！本也，撫方夏之大，保天下之室家而為王，固將以為天地神人之主乎！夫然，則不戢不那而百辟之為憲，之綱之紀而萬民之攸𡉏，後嗣之盛何如哉？吁！此吾王之所甚願，而臣下之所拳拳者。茲室也，固永為後世之那居也與！吾於是而知詩人之善頌禱矣。愛其君而及其嗣，且先之以弄璋云者，致尚德之意也。盖德粹而後嗣賢，嗣賢而後室
translation_en:
…for the future: are these expectations not great? These palace buildings have now been completed, and a banquet is held to inaugurate them. The poet’s words of praise and prayer mean that our king’s dreams and divinations agree in their auspicious signs, and sons are born. All that we pray for today carries further hopes for the future. How could it be merely a matter of dressing them in skirts and giving them jade tablets to play with? They will possess the full splendor of ceremonial dress and clearly display the distinctions marked by its insignia and colors. The scarlet knee apron is worn by the principal line of the royal house; hanging down to cover the knees, it signifies an exalted ritual rank. Beneath the dragon robe, how magnificent it looks! The yellow-red knee apron is worn by the collateral branches; fastened at the thighs, it establishes the distinctions of rank and dignity. Against the embroidered skirt, how brilliantly it shines! Thus the succession to the ancestral sacrifices is properly ordered, and the position of the worthy heir is securely entrusted; the ducal clan multiplies, and distinctions of status and duty are clear from the outset. How excellent the royal descendants will be!

Accordingly, their dress matches their rank, and their rank distinguishes their stations. Those of the collateral branches receive grants of thatch and earth conferring a fief, establish a ruling house within a state, and become its lords. Surely their strength will serve as protective walls and bulwarks! Those of the principal line govern the vast central realm, preserve the households of all under Heaven, and become kings. Surely they will thereby preside over the rites to Heaven, Earth, and the spirits, and rule over humankind! Thus, “neither restrained nor abundant” [?], they become models for the many lords; providing guiding principles and order, they become that upon which the myriad people find repose [?]. How flourishing the royal descendants will be!

Ah! This is what our king most deeply desires and what his subjects cherish with devoted concern. This palace will surely remain forever a spacious dwelling for later generations! From this I understand the poet’s skill in praise and prayer. His love for his ruler extends to the ruler’s descendants; moreover, by first speaking of their playing with jade tablets, he conveys the intention of honoring virtue. For only when virtue is pure will the descendants be worthy, and only when the descendants are worthy will the household…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
下一統治安之福也非賴先王之休何以至是
哉此商人祭祀宗廟之樂也其意若曰惟我先
后受天之命既固且安矣諸侯之臣服亦久且
遠矣則今日之天下豈非至治之時乎彼邦畿
者我商邑也天子居焉宗廟在焉固曰尊矣而
其地也方千里焉耳政令出焉表極係焉固曰
重矣而其制也儉於千里焉耳茲地也固天子
之所自治實民庶之所同居農受廛於斯工執
藝於斯近耿光以作息者盖廬井之相接焉商
===
化居於斯賈居賄於斯環景亳以聚處者盖鷄
犬之相聞焉若夫自邦畿而達之四方五百里
侯服也又五百里綏服也式廓之增土宇為之
版章矣五百里要服也又五百里荒服也幅員
之廣殷土為之芒芒矣四極之外環有海也以
經以緯何地而不歸吾之統乎四海之內無非
土也以廣以輪何者而不在吾之疆乎此實無
外之治而後人無疆之休也先王之功德何其
盛矣哉抑古帝王之德皆以文為盛書稱堯曰

藝於斯近耿光以作息者蓋廬井之相接焉商

化居於斯賈居貯於斯環景亳以聚處者蓋與
犬之相聞焉若夫自邦畿而達之四方五百里
侯服也又五百里綏服也式廓之增土宇為之
販章矣五百里要服也又五百里荒服也幅員
之廣殷土為之芒芒矣四極之外環有海也以
經以緯何地而不歸吾之統乎四海之內無非
土也以廣以輪何者而不在吾之疆乎此實無
外之治而後人無疆之休也先王之功德何其
盛矣哉抑古帝王之德皆以文為盛書稱堯曰
punctuated: 下一統治安之福也，非賴先王之休，何以至是哉？此商人祭祀宗廟之樂也。其意若曰：「惟我先后，受天之命，既固且安矣；諸侯之臣服，亦久且遠矣。則今日之天下，豈非至治之時乎？彼邦畿者，我商邑也。天子居焉，宗廟在焉，固曰尊矣，而其地也方千里焉耳；政令出焉，表極係焉，固曰重矣，而其制也儉於千里焉耳。茲地也，固天子之所自治，實民庶之所同居。農受廛於斯，工執藝於斯，近耿光以作息者，盖廬井之相接焉；商化居於斯，賈居賄於斯，環景亳以聚處者，盖鷄犬之相聞焉。若夫自邦畿而達之四方，五百里侯服也，又五百里綏服也，式廓之增，土宇為之版章矣；五百里要服也，又五百里荒服也，幅員之廣，殷土為之芒芒矣。四極之外，環有海也，以經以緯，何地而不歸吾之統乎？四海之內，無非土也，以廣以輪，何者而不在吾之疆乎？此實無外之治，而後人無疆之休也。先王之功德，何其盛矣哉！」抑古帝王之德，皆以文為盛。《書》稱堯曰：
translation_en:
…the blessings of unity, good government, and peace throughout the realm. Without the beneficence of the former kings, how could this have been attained? This is the music used by the people of Shang when offering sacrifices in the ancestral temple. Its meaning is as if to say: “Our former sovereigns received Heaven’s mandate, which became firm and secure; the allegiance of the regional lords has likewise endured long and extended far. Is not the realm today therefore enjoying an age of consummate government? That royal domain is our capital of Shang. The Son of Heaven resides there, and the ancestral temples stand there. It is assuredly exalted, yet its territory measures only a thousand li square. Government commands issue from it, and there the standard and guiding center reside. It is assuredly important, yet its prescribed extent is confined to a thousand li [?].

“This land is indeed governed directly by the Son of Heaven, but it is also where the common people dwell together. Farmers receive their homesteads here, and artisans practice their crafts here. Those who work and rest close to the sovereign’s brilliant radiance occupy adjoining dwellings and fields. Traveling merchants exchange goods here, and settled traders store their wares here. Those who cluster around great Bo live close enough to hear one another’s chickens and dogs.

“Extending outward from the royal domain in all four directions, there are five hundred li of the lords’ zone, followed by another five hundred li of the pacification zone. Through this progressive expansion, the territory becomes broadly and distinctly established [?]. There are five hundred li of the zone of restraint, followed by another five hundred li of the wilderness zone. Such is the breadth of its extent that the lands of Yin stretch boundlessly. Beyond the four extremities, seas encircle the world. Measuring north to south and east to west, what land does not come under our unified rule? Within the four seas, all is land. Across its breadth and extent, what lies outside our borders? This is truly a government that leaves nothing beyond its reach, and an inexhaustible blessing for later generations. How magnificent were the achievements and virtue of the former kings!”

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
文思舜曰文明禹曰文命而此詩所頌於湯於
武丁皆稱武無乃啓後王黷武之心與是不然
蓋商之業以武剏及盤庚浸弱之後而武丁復
以武興詩人之意無亦創往事而頌成功焉耳
若長發聖敬日躋云者則又以文頌湯矣夫武
以戡亂文以守成斯帝王之全德也有天下者
宜鑒于兹
春秋
夏公及宋公遇于清隱公四年
郭鋆
===

遠此禮猶有存者自是以往遂亡之矣夫子所以惡

…“cultured and thoughtful”; of Shun it says “cultured and enlightened,” and of Yu, “his civilizing influence spread abroad.” Yet this poem praises both Tang and Wu Ding for martial prowess. Might this not encourage later kings to indulge in warfare? This is not so. The Shang enterprise was founded through military force; following its gradual decline from the time of Pan Geng, Wu Ding again revived it through military force. The poet’s intention was perhaps merely to take warning from past events and praise accomplished achievements. As for the words “his sagely reverence rose daily” in Long Development (Chang fa), these, in turn, praise Tang’s civil virtues. Military prowess quells disorder, while civil virtue preserves established achievements: together these constitute the complete virtue of emperors and kings. Those who possess All-under-Heaven should take this as their mirror.

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
私為遇名託於古而實則異者聖人謹禮得無
致意也哉春秋之初魯隱宋殤將尋宿之盟而
為清之遇豈不自謂古有是禮可無勤有司而
隣好以修乎君子則曰禮國之紀也故嘉禮不
野合以昭度也古所謂遇盖出於邂逅而且有
賓主之辨二君私為之約則交際之頃果誰適
主乎敬禮之輿也故禮有竭情盡慎以宣誠也
古之為禮盖雖當造次而亦存恭肅之心二君
志於簡略則情文之際其何以觀乎事已申於
===
前定名則託於不期乃不知國君出疆必具官
設衛所以別嫌明微爾而可舉動無節至此耶
噫草莽之委識者所耻殤則上公隱則諸侯皆
國人之所矜式者顧弗能慎如君道何內懷慢
易之心外飾草次之具乃不知兩君相見必七
介三揖所以昭德洽情爾而可禮讓不崇如是
耶噫秕稗之辱君子不屑宋賓王家魯秉周禮
固天下之所觀望者而且弗謹如先德何故春
秋託始於清之遇而書及若曰以此及彼然也

punctuated: 私為遇，名託於古而實則異者，聖人謹禮，得無致意也哉？春秋之初，魯隱、宋殤將尋宿之盟，而為清之遇，豈不自謂古有是禮，可無勤有司而隣好以修乎？君子則曰：禮，國之紀也。故嘉禮不野合，以昭度也。古所謂遇，盖出於邂逅，而且有賓主之辨。二君私為之約，則交際之頃，果誰適主乎？敬，禮之輿也。故禮有竭情盡慎，以宣誠也。古之為禮，盖雖當造次，而亦存恭肅之心。二君志於簡略，則情文之際，其何以觀乎？事已申於前，定名則託於不期，乃不知國君出疆，必具官設衛，所以別嫌明微爾，而可舉動無節至此耶？噫！草莽之委，識者所耻。殤則上公，隱則諸侯，皆國人之所矜式者，顧弗能慎，如君道何？內懷慢易之心，外飾草次之具，乃不知兩君相見，必七介三揖，所以昭德洽情爾，而可禮讓不崇如是耶？噫！秕稗之辱，君子不屑。宋賓王家，魯秉周禮，固天下之所觀望者，而且弗謹，如先德何？故春秋託始於清之遇，而書及，若曰以此及彼然也。
translation_en:
…a privately arranged encounter, invoking ancient precedent in name but differing from it in substance. Could the Sage, scrupulous about ritual, fail to give this his attention? Early in the Spring and Autumn period, Duke Yin of Lu and Duke Shang of Song intended to renew the covenant at Su and held their encounter at Qing. Did they not tell themselves that antiquity provided for such a rite, allowing them to cultivate friendly relations between neighboring states without troubling the responsible officials? Yet the gentleman says: Ritual is the ordering framework of the state. Thus, ceremonies of friendly intercourse are not held as gatherings in the open countryside: this makes proper standards manifest. What the ancients called an “encounter” arose from a chance meeting, and even then distinguished guest from host. When the two rulers privately arranged their meeting, who, at the moment of their intercourse, was actually to act as host?

Reverence is the vehicle of ritual. Thus ritual requires the fullest expression of feeling and the utmost care, to make sincerity manifest. In performing rites, the ancients maintained a respectful and solemn heart even amid haste. When these two rulers aimed at abbreviation, what worthy example could be seen in the relation between their feelings and their ceremonial forms? The business had already been set out beforehand, yet in naming it they pretended that it was unplanned. Did they not know that when a ruler crosses his state's borders, he must have the full complement of officials and an established guard, precisely to distinguish circumstances that invite suspicion and clarify subtle points of propriety? Could their conduct be so utterly without restraint?

Alas! The degradation of being left amid wild grasses is something discerning people regard as shameful. Shang was a senior duke, and Yin a feudal lord: both were men whom the people of their states looked up to as models. Yet they could not exercise due care. What did this do to the way of the ruler? Inwardly they harbored careless and disrespectful thoughts; outwardly they made a display of hastily assembled ceremonial arrangements. Did they not know that when two rulers meet, there must be seven attendants and three bows, precisely to manifest virtue and bring their feelings into harmony? Could they fail so completely to honor ritual and deference?

Alas! The humiliation of being treated as chaff and weeds is something the gentleman disdains. Song held the standing of a guest of the royal house, while Lu upheld the rites of Zhou. They were certainly states to which all under Heaven looked for an example. Yet they too failed to exercise care. What did this do to the virtue of their predecessors? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals takes the encounter at Qing as its initial instance and writes “joined,” as though saying that this ruler went to join that one.

translation_en:
…for it condemns their complete disregard for the rites governing meetings between rulers. Alas! When sincerity is not conveyed, its carriage breaks down; when the carriage breaks down, ritual follows it into ruin. When proper standards are not made manifest, the ordering principles fall into confusion; with these in confusion, on what can the state depend? At this, the gentleman cannot but lament deeply. In Zhou’s flourishing days, ritual served as a barrier against wrongdoing in the most comprehensive manner. When Zhou declined, departures from ritual likewise became extreme: this was the source of disorder. In compiling the Classic, the Sage attended scrupulously to ritual in its smallest details. Later, when assisting the ruler of Lu at the meeting at Jiagu, he called off the banquet in the open countryside, and Qi submitted. Was this not clear evidence of its efficacy? Thus it is said: only the Sage understood that ritual could never be dispensed with.
“In spring, in the first month of the royal calendar, they fortified Chuqiu.” Second year of Duke Xi. “The men of Qin attacked Jin.” Third year of Duke Wen.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Acting Vice Director: “By citing the Classic and bringing its commentaries together, the essay explains where the two hegemons violated established rules and righteousness, leaving no loophole through which they might be exonerated. Someone without a historian’s talent could hardly attain this.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Compiler: “It develops the meaning of the two commentaries without the slightest strain. Recorded as a model for those who arrange wording and juxtapose events.”
Comment by Examiner Guo, Academician: “The wording is precise and the meaning fully expressed. This is writing that delivers a decisive judgment.”
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Academician: “Here is someone skilled in arranging wording and juxtaposing events.”
When a hegemon arrogates the authority to enfeoff, the Spring and Autumn Annals corrects him according to established rules; when men from distant lands repeat their transgressions, the Spring and Autumn Annals censures them according to righteousness. Thus Duke Huan of Qi’s enfeoffment of Wei violated established rules, and Duke Mu of Qin’s retaliation against Jin violated righteousness…

也春秋備書而其罪見矣夫詩録木瓜曰美齊

何詩之異乎盖周制凡封國有大宗伯司几筵
之禮其策命則内史也于時諸侯之專封者鮮

punctuated:
也。《春秋》備書，而其罪見矣。夫《詩》録《木瓜》，曰美齊桓也。然而城楚丘也，經不書公，若不有其事，是何《詩》之異乎？盖周制，凡封國，有大宗伯司几筵之禮，其策命則内史也。于時諸侯之專封者鮮矣。彼衛戴失國，野廬於漕，桓也率衆往遷，厚見周慎。使能請命於朝，則王制所建，誰復議之？顧乃徼惠於康叔，市德於文公，擅干封錫之典，無復奏報之義，遂使甲士乗馬，戍之自齊；祭服重錦，歸之自齊。則固不知守度正分，而以攘善樹恩為功矣。君子謂此舉猶竊粟而散之，其功雖高，無足道者。厥後葵丘之命，無有封而不告，吁，亦晚矣！故《春秋》微之，微之者，罪其專也。乃若《木瓜》，則美衛人之報爾。
夫《書》録《秦誓》，曰善秦穆也。然而伐晋也，經特人公，若不有其爵，復何《書》之異乎？盖《大易》於《損》卦，有君子懲忿窒欲之象，其曰：「損，德之修也。」于時諸侯之知德者鮮矣。彼殽師一敗，三帥見囚，穆也引咎自誓，悔心遽萌。使能堅忍不貳，則令圖所啓，天將賛之。顧乃一誤
translation_en:
…was unrighteous. The Spring and Autumn Annals records everything, and their guilt becomes apparent. The Book of Odes includes “Quince” (Mugua), said to praise Duke Huan of Qi. Yet when Chu Qiu was fortified, the Classic did not name the duke, as though he had had no part in the undertaking. Why does it differ from the Odes? Under Zhou institutions, whenever a state was enfeoffed, the Minister of Rites supervised the ceremonies involving stools and mats, while the Interior Scribe handled the written investiture. In those days, few regional lords presumed to enfeoff states on their own authority. When Dai of Wei [?] lost his state and lodged in the countryside at Cao, Duke Huan led his forces there to relocate him, displaying great solicitude and care. Had he requested authorization from the royal court, the settlement would have been established under royal institutions: who could then have criticized it? Instead, he sought credit for favors to Kang Shu and purchased a reputation for benevolence from Duke Wen. He presumptuously encroached upon the institutions governing enfeoffment and grants, entirely disregarding his obligation to report to the throne. Thus armored soldiers and teams of four horses came from Qi to defend Wei, and sacrificial robes and layered brocades were sent from Qi. He clearly did not understand how to observe established limits and maintain the proper distinctions of rank, but counted appropriating credit and cultivating gratitude as achievements. The gentleman judges this undertaking to be like stealing grain and distributing it: however great the achievement, it merits no praise. Later, the injunction at Kui Qiu stipulated that no enfeoffment should take place without being reported. Alas, that too came late! Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals obscures his role; in doing so, it condemns his usurpation of authority. As for “Quince,” it merely praises the gratitude shown by the people of Wei.
The Book of Documents includes “The Oath of Qin” (Qin shi), said to commend Duke Mu of Qin. Yet when he attacked Jin, the Classic designated the duke simply as a man, as though he possessed no noble title. Why, again, does it differ from the Documents? In the Great Book of Changes, the hexagram “Decrease” (Sun) presents the image of the gentleman restraining anger and curbing desires. It says: “Decrease is the cultivation of virtue.” In those days, few regional lords understood virtue. After the army’s defeat at Yao, when its three commanders were taken prisoner, Duke Mu accepted the blame and made a solemn pledge, and a repentant heart promptly emerged. Had he remained steadfast and not repeated his fault, Heaven would have assisted the good designs thus begun. Instead, a single error…

…those grounded in the root [?], record them.

Comment by Associate Examiner Gong, Compiler: “Among passages in the Record of Music that discuss music in terms of feeling, patterned expression, and practical effects together, this alone treats them in detail. There is no shortage of writers in the examination hall, but their treatments are cursory [?]. This answer alone is clear, classically elegant, and refined; its handling of the essential points particularly displays strength of composition. It should be recorded as a model.”

To be rooted in the heart and able to move others: herein lies the way the former kings made music. Music has never been able to move others without first issuing from one’s own heart. If we seek the former kings’ way of making music through this principle, what could remain unknowable? Now music is that from which feelings arise, and it is indeed something human feeling cannot do without. When correct music is made, it can move people wherever it finds expression. Yet could it lack a root? Thus, before external things have stirred us, we must preserve the clear and undivided substance of our being, thereby establishing its capacity to respond fittingly. When the great root is established and the universally applicable Way is put into practice, all feelings are correct, and the root of music is established.

Once feelings have been aroused, they are blended and harmonized through instruments and numerical measures, giving manifest adornment to the measured divisions of melodies. When the five notes are made correct and the eight classes of instrumental sound are given expression, everything is harmonized, and music’s patterned expression is complete. When pitches are attuned and rhythms brought into accord, there are the finely articulated arrangements and measured proportions, and the enduring order of leading and answering, high and low tones. title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
不相奪若文采錯雜而不相亂也則樂之無不
和可知矣此其所以用之宗廟用之閨門則父
子君臣之至親至嚴者皆有以比其類而合之
而和親和敬者也用之邦國用之鄉黨則萬民
之至疎至眾者皆有以聯其情而屬之而和順
和睦者也由是觀之則先王之作樂也非以導
欲也所以平天下之情者在是矣非以飾喜也
所以宣天下之化者在是矣其存之也至靜其
出之也至和故其為用至廣而其為感至神也
===
先王立樂之方寧復有餘蘊哉蓋發於吾心而
感於人心者無二理也善觀樂者亦於此求之
雖然樂之始固本之人情而作而人情之終亦
必由樂而治則情為作樂之本而樂乃治情之
要也故曰樂者樂也人情之所不能免也舜之
命夔曰八音克諧無相奪倫神人以和嗚呼先
王作樂之道盡之矣師乙之告子貢曰動巳而
天地應焉四時和焉星辰理焉萬物育焉則樂
之和天地且不違也而况於人乎况於鬼神乎
