王作樂之道盡之矣師乙之告子貢曰動已而
天地應焉四時和焉星辰理焉萬物育焉則樂
之和天地且不違也而況於人乎況於鬼神乎
punctuated:
不相奪，若文采錯雜而不相亂也，則樂之無不和可知矣。此其所以用之宗廟，用之閨門，則父子君臣之至親至嚴者，皆有以比其類而合之，而和親和敬者也；用之邦國，用之鄉黨，則萬民之至疎至眾者，皆有以聯其情而屬之，而和順和睦者也。由是觀之，則先王之作樂也，非以導欲也，所以平天下之情者在是矣；非以飾喜也，所以宣天下之化者在是矣。其存之也至靜，其出之也至和，故其為用至廣，而其為感至神也。先王立樂之方，寧復有餘蘊哉？蓋發於吾心而感於人心者，無二理也。善觀樂者，亦於此求之。
雖然，樂之始固本之人情而作，而人情之終亦必由樂而治，則情為作樂之本，而樂乃治情之要也。故曰：「樂者，樂也，人情之所不能免也。」舜之命夔曰：「八音克諧，無相奪倫，神人以和。」嗚呼！先王作樂之道盡之矣。師乙之告子貢曰：「動巳而天地應焉，四時和焉，星辰理焉，萬物育焉。」則樂之和，天地且不違也，而况於人乎？况於鬼神乎？
translation_en:
…without encroaching upon one another, like intermingled colors and patterns that do not fall into disorder. Thus we can understand that music is harmonious in every respect. This is why, when it is employed in ancestral temples and within the household, the supremely intimate and solemn relationships of father and son, ruler and minister, are brought together according to their kinds, producing harmony in affection and reverence. When it is employed in states and local communities, the people, however distant from one another and however numerous, have their feelings linked and are bound together, producing harmony in obedience and mutual amity. Viewed in this light, the former kings made music not to lead people into desire: herein lay the means of bringing equilibrium to the feelings of all under Heaven. They did not make it to embellish pleasure: herein lay the means of spreading moral transformation throughout the world. While held within, it is supremely still; when expressed, it is supremely harmonious. Thus its application is supremely broad, and its power to move people supremely wondrous. Could anything remain undisclosed in the former kings’ method of establishing music? For what issues from our own hearts and moves the hearts of others operates by one and the same principle. Those who understand how to examine music also seek its meaning here.
Nevertheless, although music was originally created on the basis of human feelings, those feelings must ultimately be brought into order through music. Feelings are therefore the foundation for making music, while music is the essential means of ordering feelings. Thus it is said: “Music is joy, something human feelings cannot do without.” Shun’s command to Kui states: “Let the eight kinds of instrumental sound achieve harmony, without encroaching upon one another’s proper order, so that spirits and humans may be in harmony.” Ah! This exhausts the Way by which the former kings made music. Music Master Yi told Zigong: “When one moves oneself [?], Heaven and Earth respond; the four seasons harmonize, the stars follow their proper order, and the myriad things are nurtured.” Thus even Heaven and Earth do not run counter to the harmony of music. How much less would human beings do so? How much less the ghosts and spirits?

Only a sage can fully realize the way of benevolence toward the people and thereby treat them as his children. To fulfill both reverence and affection is the gentleman’s way of showing benevolence toward the people. Who but a sage could attain this? text:
其子者矣莫親於母也於民而說安之則有惨
怛之愛厚莫重焉真如慈母之保赤子者矣夫
唯有父道之尊也則雖不必生之為父而吾之
有馮有翼者有以大丕冒之仁民亦莫不尊之
如父也唯有母道之親也則雖不必育之為母
而吾之引養引恬者有以同顧復之德民亦莫
不親之如母也其立於民上而為民父母也何
愧之有若是者夫豈人之所可能哉盖德盛則
化自神仁熟而施斯普剛健中正體乾道也而
範圍之下自合萬物而兼濟之則天下之民有
不仰之若父母乎聰明聖智達天德也而曲成
之下自囿四海而無外焉故凡有血氣者莫不
尊親矣是乃治化之極功聖人之能事也非聖
人而求其尊親之兼盡也難矣詩之所謂凱弟

By bringing the people joy and security, the ruler shows a tender, compassionate love unsurpassed in its depth, truly like a loving mother protecting her infant. Because he possesses the dignity proper to a father, although he need not have begotten the people to be their father, the support and assistance he provides magnify his all-encompassing benevolence, and the people all revere him as a father. Because he possesses the affection proper to a mother, although he need not have reared the people to be their mother, the lasting nourishment and tranquillity he provides match the virtue of a mother's watchful care, and the people all love him as a mother. Standing above the people and serving as their father and mother, what could he have to be ashamed of? Yet how could such an achievement lie within ordinary human capacity?
When virtue is abundant, its transforming influence naturally becomes wondrous; when benevolence is fully matured, its benefits extend everywhere. Firm and vigorous, balanced and correct, he embodies the Way of Qian, Heaven. Within his encompassing order, he naturally embraces all things and brings aid to them alike. Could any of the people under Heaven fail to look up to him as a parent? Perceptive and discerning, sagely and wise, he comprehends Heaven's virtue. Through bringing each thing to fulfilment according to its particular nature, he naturally embraces all within the Four Seas, leaving nothing outside. Thus all beings possessed of blood and breath revere and love him. This is the highest achievement of transformative government, the work of which a sage is capable. For someone who is not a sage to seek to fulfil both the roles of revered father and beloved mother is indeed difficult!
The Odes speaks of the “kind and amiable gentleman, father and mother of the people.” Apart from the sage, to whom could this description apply? Moreover, the Documents says: “One who is truly perceptive and discerning becomes the great sovereign; the great sovereign becomes father and mother of the people.” It also says: “The Son of Heaven serves as father and mother of the people, thereby becoming king of all under Heaven.” Truly, none but a sage can serve as father and mother to these people! In this chapter, the Master discusses how difficult it is for the ruler's Way to fulfil benevolence completely, and directs his attention particularly to Shun…

When a righteous ruler sets all under Heaven aright through righteousness, none fail to follow him in practicing righteousness, and no righteous person puts his ruler last. This is what is called the greatest benefit. When ruler and ministers engage with one another through benevolence and righteousness, the greatest benefit follows. Through these, one perfects oneself, perfects one's ruler, and serves all under Heaven. This, indeed, is how a minister gives his whole heart and is loyal to his ruler. Ministers who cherish benevolence and righteousness and those who cherish profit alike serve a ruler. Yet those who cherish profit lead their ruler toward desire and ultimately into danger, while those who cherish benevolence and righteousness lead their ruler toward the Way and ultimately into security. Is the distinction between benefit and harm not perfectly clear? This is why those who cherish benevolence and righteousness are skilled in guiding their ruler and exemplify the highest loyalty.

Someone may say: “The nature endowed with benevolence and righteousness cannot be altered; it is shared by everyone. Yet those who serve rulers in this age all abandon it and cherish only profit. Perhaps, because their ruler's nature is obscured by desire, they accommodate him and follow his preferences; they also do so merely to benefit themselves.” Alas! In serving his ruler, a gentleman need only give his utmost. Complying with the ruler's desires is a lesser form of respect for him; following the Way is the greater form. Whether employed or not, he follows this same principle. Never has there been sincerity that failed to move others. How could one…

也苟求于利將不得之于此而得之于彼其為

仁義之其于義利得失之辨審矣信乎人臣事

利言也？彼宋牼者，小變其說，以搆兵為不利，罷兵為利，以求遇於秦楚之君。所利不同，為利一也。苟求于利，將不得之于此而得之于彼，其為利之害一也。孟子正人心，扶世道，欲易其懷而仁義之，其于義利得失之辨審矣，信乎人臣事君者之大法也！雖然，欲正乎君，必先乎其身。未有身體仁義而不能以仁義事其君者，亦未有不能于其身而能善其君者。反諸身而仁義焉，其道如之何？孟子固曰：「人皆有所不忍，達之於其所忍，仁也；人皆有所不為，達之於其所為，義也。人能充無欲害人之心，而仁不可勝用也；人能充無穿窬之心，而義不可勝用也。」即是深求而實體之，仁義之道得矣。仁義之道得，而君可正矣。故曰：「惟大人為能格君心之非。」

擬賜御製欽
translation_en:
… speak in terms of profit? That Song Keng made a slight alteration to his argument, treating the waging of war as unprofitable and the cessation of war as profitable, in order to gain acceptance with the rulers of Qin and Chu. Although the benefits sought differed, the pursuit of profit was the same. If one seeks profit, one may fail to obtain it here yet obtain it elsewhere; the harm caused by pursuing profit remains the same. Mencius sought to rectify people’s hearts and uphold the moral order of the world, wishing to change what they cherished and turn them toward benevolence and righteousness. His discrimination between righteousness and profit, and between gain and loss, was exact indeed. This is truly the great rule by which a minister should serve his ruler!

Nevertheless, anyone wishing to rectify his ruler must begin with himself. No one who personally embodies benevolence and righteousness has ever been unable to serve his ruler through them; nor has anyone unable to practice them himself ever been able to make his ruler good. What is the way to turn back upon oneself and practice benevolence and righteousness? Mencius indeed said: “Everyone has things he cannot bear to do; extending this feeling to what he can bear to do is benevolence. Everyone has things he will not do; extending this restraint to what he does do is righteousness. If a person can fully develop his heart’s unwillingness to harm others, his benevolence will be inexhaustible in its application. If a person can fully develop his unwillingness to break through walls or climb over them to steal, his righteousness will be inexhaustible in its application.” By investigating these principles deeply and truly embodying them, one attains the Way of benevolence and righteousness. Once that Way is attained, the ruler can be rectified. Thus it is said: “Only a great man can rectify what is wrong in the ruler’s heart.”

圜丘肇祀，天心響應乎休徵；睿藻敷文，帝德靈承於祗若。煥龍章之普錫，倬雲漢之昭回，喜溢縉紳，光踰琬琰。臣等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首上言：伏以幽明之理雖微，臨下有赫；對越之忱彌篤，申福無疆。欽昊格而蓂莢生，時幾勅而卿雲見；隨車甘雨，應湯德之日新；同穎嘉禾，符周敬之作所。慨帝王之響既息，而昭事之道遂微。漢瑞紀年，徒矜文飾；宋圖示象，何補身心？禮樂待人而行，神聖應時以出。
恭惟皇帝陛下，道隆峻極，德懋重華，基命協麟趾之祥，宅天眷
translation_en:
…Sacrifice was inaugurated at the Circular Mound, and Heaven’s will responded through auspicious signs. Your sagacious compositions unfolded in writing, and your imperial virtue reverently received Heaven’s wondrous favor. Resplendent are the imperial writings bestowed upon all; brilliant as the Milky Way, their radiance shines abroad. Joy overflows among the officials, and their luster surpasses fine jade. We, your servants, are truly joyful and truly delighted. Bowing our heads to the ground and knocking our foreheads upon it, we submit these words:
We humbly consider that, although the principles governing the unseen and visible realms are subtle, Heaven looks down with manifest majesty. As sincerity in reverently attending Heaven grows ever deeper, blessings are extended without limit. Reverence reaches august Heaven, and the mingjia calendrical plant springs forth; the affairs of the moment are put in order, and auspicious clouds appear. Sweet rain following the royal carriage answered to Tang’s daily renewal of virtue; auspicious grain with joined ears accorded with Zhou’s reverence in establishing its proper place [?]. Alas, once the echoes of the ancient emperors and kings had faded, the Way of illustriously serving Heaven consequently declined. The Han named reign periods after auspicious signs, merely vaunting ornamental display; the Song presented portents in pictures—what benefit did these bring to personal conduct or the mind? Rites and music await the right person to put them into practice; a divinely sagacious ruler emerges in response to the times.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor has exalted the Way to its loftiest summit and brought virtue to a flourishing state rivaling Chonghua, the sage Shun. In establishing the Mandate, you accord with the auspicious sign of the qilin’s hoof; you abide in Heaven’s favor…

punctuated: 龍飛之化，河再清于二紀，瑞疊獻于四方。學有緝熈，心存敬一。非天子固不議禮，惟王者能自得師。及庚寅之仲冬，舉泰壇之禋祀，奠陳蒼璧，樂備黃鍾。燔燎靄而明德昭升，醴齊馨而有孚顒若。禮崇大報，復曠典於千年；誠假居歆，錫嘉祥於期月。天乳騰輝於氐北，靈液委潤於湘南。適當華渚之鄉，況值玄宫之勝。珠聯玉綴，紛草木之增榮；雪瑩脂凝，賁山川之炫采。維茲寶露，允協貞符。爰舉告虔之儀，益彰備物之養。甘香注之瑶斝，精華承以金觥。祇薦宗祊，祈滋稼穡；敬呈慈闕，冀永年齡。尤託宸翰以撝謙，若銘丹書而志戒。成功惟歸帝，善則稱
translation_en:
…the transforming influence of the dragon’s ascent to sovereignty. The Yellow River has twice run clear within two twelve-year cycles, and auspicious signs have repeatedly been presented from the four quarters. Your learning advances in continuing illumination; your heart maintains reverent singleness of purpose. None but the Son of Heaven may deliberate upon rites; only a true king can himself find a teacher. In midwinter of the gengyin year [1530], you performed the pure sacrifice at the Great Altar. The azure jade disk was laid out as an offering, and the music was fully provided in the Yellow Bell pitch. Amid the haze of burning offerings, luminous virtue rose resplendent; the sweet sacrificial liquor was fragrant, and sincerity was manifest in solemn reverence. The rites honored the great repayment to Heaven, restoring a ceremony neglected for a thousand years. Your sincerity reached the divine presence and won acceptance, and auspicious blessings were bestowed within a month.

Heavenly milk shone north of the Di constellation, and numinous liquid spread its moisture south of the Xiang River. It appeared precisely in the region of Huazhu, and moreover at the splendid site of the imperial burial chamber. Like linked pearls and strung jade, it richly enhanced the glory of plants and trees; bright as snow and congealed as fat, it adorned mountains and rivers with dazzling color. This precious dew truly accorded with an authentic auspicious sign. Thus you performed the ceremony announcing your devotion, further displaying the fullness of your filial provision. Its sweet fragrance was poured into jade cups, its pure essence received in golden goblets. Reverently you offered it at the ancestral temple, praying that it would nourish the crops; respectfully you presented it at the Empress Dowager’s palace, hoping to prolong her years. Above all, through your imperial writings you expressed humility, as though inscribing admonitions from the Cinnabar Writing and keeping its warnings in mind. Accomplishment is attributed solely to the Supreme Sovereign; goodness is ascribed to…

親。記垂三百言，渾渾乎典謨至訓；頌盈數十韻，洋洋乎風雅徽音。玉振金聲，奎璧映圖書之府；天經地緯，龜龍效河洛之文。夙夜勉修，誠溢言外；雨暘時若，望切淵衷。徵五福以綏兆民，登来牟而乂家國。荷元樞之不息，仰昊極之難名。是誠仁孝達乎天人，而明聖兼夫述作者也。
臣等叨拜宸章之寵，欣沾湛露之恩，敢不仰悉眷懷，俯攄忠悃？靖共有位，思體國以體萬民；齊明此心，期格君以格上帝。伏願永綏殷薦，益篤丕休，處豐而宜日中，保泰以臨天下。
translation_en:
…to his parent. The record extends to three hundred words, profound in its supreme teachings like the Canons and Counsels; the eulogy fills several dozen rhymes, abundant in its beautiful strains like the Airs and Elegantiae. Jade chimes and bronze bells resound; the constellations Kui and Bi shine upon the repository of books. Heaven’s warp and earth’s weft are ordered; the tortoise and dragon present the patterns of the Yellow River and the Luo River. Your earnest cultivation, pursued morning and night, conveys a sincerity beyond the words themselves; the hope that rain and sunshine will come in their proper seasons lies deep within your heart. You summon the five blessings to bring peace to the myriad people, and bring wheat and barley to maturity to order the ruling house and the state. You receive the blessings of Heaven’s unceasing workings and look reverently toward its supreme height, which words cannot describe. Truly, your benevolence and filial piety reach both Heaven and humanity, while your enlightened sagacity unites the accomplishments of transmitter and creator.
We, your servants, have unworthily received the honor of your imperial composition and rejoice to be bathed in favor like the abundant dew. How could we fail to comprehend your solicitous concern above and express our loyal devotion below? Serving reverently in our offices, we seek to care for the state and thereby care for all its people; purifying and illuminating our hearts, we hope to move our sovereign and thereby move the Lord on High. We humbly wish that you may forever enjoy peace through ample offerings and further deepen your great blessings; that, dwelling amid abundance, you may fittingly be as the sun at midday, and preserve prosperity as you preside over all under Heaven.…

Associate Examiner Ouyang, Compiler, comments: He grounds his argument in emulating Heaven and the imperial ancestor; his insight is distinctive, his spirit abundant, and his language magnificent. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Associate Examiner Wang, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: Since antiquity, sages establishing government have transformed the people through virtue, resorting to punishment only when unavoidable. Our sagely ancestor bequeathed admonitions and established moral instruction, making punishments clear to support it: this was precisely the intention of the ancient sages. You have celebrated these splendid accomplishments, and at the end you repeatedly express earnest, respectful hopes for our present sovereign. Do you wish to witness the ancient ideal of government in which the people are wholly transformed and punishments are auspiciously administered? Moreover, your language and spirit are pure and elegant. You especially deserve to be recommended first.

Examiner Guo, Academician, comments: Strengthening moral instruction and exercising compassion in punishment—these were the means by which our imperial ancestor nurtured the vital energies of our sagely dynasty to the utmost. Now His Majesty attaches still greater importance to instruction and exercises still greater care in punishment, thereby deepening…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
皇祖之意豈惟天下蒙其福固可以為萬世法程而不可易者子能鋪揚
無遺豈識時務者耶
考試官學士張　批　我
皇祖盛德如天其可見者教刑二事正與天道無間我
皇上又能法
祖法天憂勤之念恒切於此子能一一道之末復有懇切忠愛之懷若有
未盡者錄以登
獻豈但為文也耶
法天以為治者成天下之業者也法
===
祖以為治者守天下之業者也今夫天春以生
萬物成之以秋皆仁也聖人教以正萬民
輔之以刑亦仁也故易曰元者善之長也
君子體仁足以長人又曰天地之大德曰
生聖人之大寶曰位何以守位曰仁春秋
繫王於天曰春王正月非法天之謂乎書
曰率乃祖攸行詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章
非法
祖之謂乎知此則知我

祖之謂乎知此則知我
punctuated:
皇祖之意，豈惟天下蒙其福，固可以為萬世法程而不可易者。子能鋪揚無遺，豈識時務者耶？
考試官學士張　批：我皇祖盛德如天，其可見者，教刑二事，正與天道無間。我皇上又能法祖法天，憂勤之念恒切於此。子能一一道之，末復有懇切忠愛之懷，若有未盡者。錄以登獻，豈但為文也耶？
法天以為治者，成天下之業者也；法祖以為治者，守天下之業者也。今夫天春以生萬物，成之以秋，皆仁也。聖人教以正萬民，輔之以刑，亦仁也。故《易》曰：「元者，善之長也。君子體仁，足以長人。」又曰：「天地之大德曰生，聖人之大寶曰位。何以守位？曰仁。」《春秋》繫王於天，曰：「春王正月。」非法天之謂乎？《書》曰：「率乃祖攸行。」《詩》曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」非法祖之謂乎？知此，則知我
translation_en:
…the intent of the imperial ancestor. How could this merely bring blessings upon all under Heaven? It can indeed serve as an unalterable model for ten thousand generations. You have expounded and celebrated it without omission. Are you not one who understands the affairs of the age?
Examiner, Academician Zhang, comments: Our imperial ancestor’s abundant virtue was like Heaven. Its visible manifestations, education and punishment, accorded perfectly with the Way of Heaven. Our Emperor can also take the ancestor and Heaven as his models; his anxious concern and diligence are constantly focused upon these matters. You have explained them one by one, and at the end you further express earnest loyalty and love, as though something still remained unsaid. We select this answer for presentation to the throne: could it be merely an exercise in composition?
Those who govern by taking Heaven as their model establish the enterprise of ruling all under Heaven; those who govern by taking their ancestors as models preserve that enterprise. Now Heaven brings the myriad things to life in spring and brings them to maturity in autumn: all this is benevolence. The sage uses education to set the myriad people right and supports it with punishments: this too is benevolence. Thus the Book of Changes says: “The originating is the foremost of goodness. The gentleman embodies benevolence and is thereby fit to lead others.” It also says: “The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is giving life; the great treasure of the sage is his position. By what does he preserve his position? By benevolence.” The Spring and Autumn Annals links the king to Heaven, saying: “Spring, the first month of the king’s calendar.” Does this not mean taking Heaven as one’s model? The Book of Documents says: “Follow what your ancestor practiced.” The Book of Odes says: “Neither erring nor forgetting, follow the old statutes.” Does this not mean taking one’s ancestor as a model? Understanding this, one understands our…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
聖祖之所以成天下萬世之業及我
皇上之所以守之者矣執事發策以
聖朝功德之盛未易殫述因舉教刑遠過前代
及
聖天子惇崇慎恤之意欲並揄揚於萬一愚也
末學惡足以知之顧嘗讀漢董仲舒之言
曰陽常居大夏以生育長養為事陰常居
大冬而積於空虛不用之地以此見天之
任德不任刑也夫教與刑皆始於虞而詳
===
於周舜命契為司徒曰敬敷五教在寬命
臯陶為士師曰欽恤明允伯夷降典折民
惟刑言先教也明于五刑以弼五教言後
刑也周之教其大者曰因民五常而施十
二教曰以鄉三物教萬民而又以八刑糾
之其不變者則屢移之觀辟雍之於樂菁
莪之樂育大比之賓興夫曰樂曰賓云者
所以待士之意何厚耶其刑之大者曰三
典五刑曰三刺三赦三宥而又以嘉石平

punctuated: 聖祖之所以成天下萬世之業，及我皇上之所以守之者矣。執事發策，以聖朝功德之盛未易殫述，因舉教刑遠過前代，及聖天子惇崇慎恤之意，欲並揄揚於萬一。愚也末學，惡足以知之？顧嘗讀漢董仲舒之言曰：「陽常居大夏，以生育長養為事；陰常居大冬，而積於空虛不用之地。以此見天之任德不任刑也。」夫教與刑，皆始於虞而詳於周。舜命契為司徒，曰：「敬敷五教，在寬。」命臯陶為士師，曰：「欽恤明允。」伯夷降典，折民惟刑，言先教也；明于五刑，以弼五教，言後刑也。周之教，其大者曰因民五常而施十二教，曰以鄉三物教萬民，而又以八刑糾之。其不變者，則屢移之。觀辟雍之於樂、菁莪之樂育、大比之賓興，夫曰樂曰賓云者，所以待士之意何厚耶！其刑之大者，曰三典五刑，曰三刺三赦三宥，而又以嘉石平
translation_en:
…how our sagely ancestor established an enterprise encompassing all under Heaven and enduring for ten thousand generations, and how our present emperor preserves it. In setting this policy question, you observed that the magnificent achievements and virtues of our sagely dynasty could not readily be recounted in full. You therefore singled out its instruction and punishments, which far surpass those of preceding dynasties, together with the sagely Son of Heaven’s intention to esteem instruction generously and administer punishment with caution and compassion, wishing to extol some tiny part of both. Ignorant as I am, and of meager learning, how could I adequately understand these matters? Yet I have read these words of Dong Zhongshu of the Han: “Yang regularly occupies high summer, taking as its task the generation, nurture, growth, and sustenance of life. Yin regularly occupies deep winter, accumulating in an empty and unused place. From this we see that Heaven relies on virtue, not punishment.”
Instruction and punishment both began under Yu and were elaborated under Zhou. Shun appointed Xie as Minister of Education, saying, “Reverently disseminate the five teachings, exercising leniency.” He appointed Gao Yao as Chief Judicial Official, saying, “Be reverent, compassionate, discerning, and fair.” That Bo Yi promulgated the statutes, and punishment brought the people to order, means that instruction came first; that the five punishments were made clear to support the five teachings means that punishment came afterward.
Among the principal features of Zhou instruction were the application of twelve teachings based on the people’s five constant moral qualities, and the instruction of all the people through the three categories of township education. Furthermore, the eight punishments were used to correct them. Those who failed to reform were repeatedly transferred elsewhere. Consider the joy of the Biyong royal academy, the joyful nurturing of talent celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood,” and the honoring and advancement of worthy men as guests at the triennial assessment. How generous was the intention toward scholars expressed in these words “joy” and “guests”!
Among the principal features of its punishments were the three penal codes and five punishments, the three consultations concerning capital sentences, the three grounds for pardon, and the three grounds for leniency. Furthermore, the fine stone was used to bring to order…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
罷民肺石達窮民若左右刑罰有五禁焉
先後刑罰有五戒焉兩造之禁訟入束矢
而後聽兩劑之禁獄入鈞金而後聽夫曰
禁曰戒云者所以慮民之意何周邪嗚呼
自是而降若漢唐宋之世雖詳畧輕重不
同而先王之意則蕩然矣洪惟我
太祖高皇帝驅逐胡元肇造區宇開
國之初不遑他務慨天下之民無教也首建
太學於京師尋立郡縣學於天下里置塾
===
以督學鄉置鐸以徇教材置鼓以會衆學
置飲射以崇禮或采名德以為模範或頒
經書以資講習雖沿宋三舍升補之法而
廩餼供具無不周至且謂
朝廷作養必使得所然後可必其成材其
諭中書省臣曰治國之要教化為先教化之道
學校為本
諭御史臺曰教化行雖閭閻可使為君子教化
廢雖中才或墜於小人

…the wayward people, while the lung stone enabled the distressed to make their grievances known. To guide the application of punishments, there were five prohibitions; to govern what preceded and followed their application, there were five admonitions. Under the requirement that both parties appear, a suit was heard only after a bundle of arrows had been deposited; under the requirement for the two documents, a case was heard only after thirty jin of metal had been deposited. How comprehensive was the concern for the people expressed in these prohibitions and admonitions! Alas! From that time onward, in such ages as the Han, Tang, and Song, although provisions differed in detail and punishments in severity, the intentions of the former kings disappeared entirely.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao expelled the Mongol Yuan and established the realm. At the dynasty’s founding, he had no leisure for other affairs. Lamenting that the people throughout the realm lacked instruction, he first established the Imperial University in the capital, and shortly afterward established prefectural and county schools throughout the realm. In each neighborhood he provided a school to oversee learning; in each township, a bell to proclaim instruction; in each village [?], a drum to assemble the people; and in the schools, ceremonial drinking and archery to honor ritual propriety. He selected men renowned for virtue to serve as models and distributed the canonical books to support lectures and study. Although he followed the Song system of promotion and admission through the three college divisions, every provision for stipends, food, and supplies was thoroughly attended to. He further held that, in nurturing talent, the court must ensure that students were suitably provided for; only then could it be certain that they would become accomplished men. He instructed the officials of the Central Secretariat: “In governing a state, moral instruction takes priority; in providing moral instruction, schools are the foundation.” He instructed the Censorate: “When moral instruction prevails, even people in the common lanes can be made into gentlemen; when moral instruction is neglected, even those of middling ability may sink to become petty men.”

Because Li Sidi had shown integrity while serving as a district magistrate, he summoned him from his place of demotion and appointed him to office. He allowed the grandfather of Cheng Tong, a student of the National University, to return from banishment to military service; released a resident of Shanyang County who had taken a beating with the heavy bamboo in his father’s stead; and pardoned Registrar Zhang Jie so that he could care for his mother.
He issued the Statutes of the Great Ming to enforce the fundamental safeguards, and established the Code of the Great Ming to transmit the fundamental laws to posterity. … his eagerness to reward. When about to impose punishment, he would forgo a full meal; if he did take one, he would dispense with music. This shows his dread of punishment. Luo Congyan of the Song said: “Benevolence and righteousness are the ruler’s methods. If he relies exclusively on benevolence, all under Heaven will love him but will not know to fear him; if he relies exclusively on righteousness, all under Heaven will fear him but will not know to love him. Benevolence may be carried to excess; righteousness must not be.” This, perhaps, is the way to care for the people.

Nevertheless, to teach is to provide an example; to follow an example is to learn. It is what all under Heaven look to as their standard. Punishment means giving form; giving form means making something fixed. Once fixed, it cannot be changed. Thus the gentleman devotes his utmost care to it. In the time of the Three Dynasties, the Son of Heaven, the dukes, and the ministers personally put virtue into practice in their high positions. Their words, conduct, and administration could all serve as models. Was this not how they taught? The Minister of Justice reported the completed judgment in a case to the king, who ordered the Three Dukes to hear it jointly. The Three Dukes then reported the completed judgment to the king. The king considered grounds for pardon three times before determining the punishment. For the Son of Heaven took cherishing life as his virtue, while the responsible officials took upholding the law as their public duty. Thus punishments were not excessive, and the people submitted willingly in their hearts. These are indeed the responsibilities of those at court who carry out Heaven’s work on its behalf. How could someone as foolish as I adequately understand them? I can only ask you to instruct me orally [?].

Second Question
Chen Tan

君信焉言也用其臣言雖不自之出而可
信焉用也盖古者今之鑒治之則也為君
而不稽於古則善惡之鑒迷而取舍之則
繆事君而不以古陳之則法戒之道隱而
獻替之意微其以格君而致治難矣此稽
古錄一書司馬文正公之所由作晦菴朱
子之欲亟進于朝而執事亦以發策之意
乎吁豈惟司馬氏爾也我不可不監于有
夏亦不可不監于有殷召公固以告于周
===

軾上陸贄之奏則亦有由然矣事焉師古

為已任其輔養君德康熈治道尤拳拳焉

Antiquity is the mirror of the present and the standard for government. If a ruler does not examine antiquity, his discernment of good and evil becomes clouded, and his standards for accepting and rejecting become mistaken. If one serves a ruler without presenting precedents from antiquity, the principles of emulation and warning become obscured, and the purpose of recommending the good and correcting the bad becomes faint. It is then difficult to rectify the ruler and bring about good government. Was this not why Sima, Lord Wenzheng, composed the Record of Investigations into Antiquity (Jigu lu), why Master Zhu of Hui’an wished urgently to present it at court, and also what prompted you, sir, to set this policy question? Taking antiquity as one’s guide in affairs is indeed an exemplary practice of emperors and kings; is speaking with supporting evidence not also a good way for ministers to enlighten their ruler? Allow me to elaborate on this in response to your discerning question.
In the middle period of the Song, the realm faced many troubles. Lord Wenzheng came forward, endowed with sincerity, integrity, and uprightness, and possessed of pure and lofty learning. He was especially devoted to nurturing his ruler’s virtue and bringing peace and flourishing to the way of government. Of all his lifelong efforts in learning, much of what he gained came from the histories. He once received an imperial command to compile the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian). …a table of contents, which he submitted together with it. Subsequently, finding this too brief, he began a Record of Essential Points (Juyao lu), but did not finish it. The present book brings together his early writings. He evidently also believed that a ruler should survey the events of former ages widely, taking encouragement and warning from them; yet historical writings were so voluminous that a ruler might sometimes lack the leisure. He therefore compiled a Chart of Successive Years (Linian tu), covering the period from the establishment of the three states of Jin to the end of the Xiande reign of the Later Zhou, and presented it to Yingzong. The events of altogether 1,362 years could thus be consulted. He also compiled a Table of the Hundred Officials (Baiguan biao), covering the period from the first year of the Song founder’s Jianlong reign to the end of Yingzong’s Zhiping reign, and presented it to Shenzong. The events of one founding emperor and four succeeding emperors, spanning 108 years, could thus be consulted.

When Zhezong ascended the throne as a young child, the Duke was promoted to chief councilor. He guided, corrected, and assisted the sovereign, untiring in his loyalty and devotion. He further compiled all the material from the inception of written records under Fuxi down to and including the dingchou year of King Weilie, supplementing what the chart and table had not covered. He gave the whole the title Record of Examining Antiquity (Jigu lu) and presented it to the throne. The course of order and disorder, rise and decline, across thousands of years was comprehensively recorded. His love for his sovereign was deep, and therefore his words were earnest; his concern for his times was profound, and therefore his explanations were detailed. Master Zhu Xi, known as Hui’an, said that his desire to serve his sovereign and father loyally had endured through three reigns before reaching fruition, and that the work could be used for reading before the emperor at the imperial lectures.

Looking now at its prefatory discussion, we find the statement: “The way of ruling men has one essential: employing men. Its virtues are three: benevolence, discernment, and martial resolve. Its five measures [?] are founding the enterprise, preserving its accomplishments, gradual decline, restoration, and…”

Because the Way may be lost or attained, government displays disorder or good order; because virtue may be high or low, achievements are great or small; because ability may be good or bad, eras flourish or decline. His purpose was earnest and devoted, and thus his scrutiny was close; his ability and judgment were clear and upright, and thus his assessments and selections were discerning. text:
乎巧譎苛察而知道義識安危别賢愚辨
是非知於是乎廣矣不尚乎強暴亢厲而

又嘗竊聞之自夫明良之遇既遠而尊卑

經筵臨御之時

乎巧譎苛察，而知道義，識安危，别賢愚，辨是非，知於是乎廣矣；不尚乎強暴亢厲，而姦不能惑，佞不能移，武於是乎立矣。中興之業，不其益有光哉？此固執事之意也。愚又嘗竊聞之，自夫明良之遇既遠，而尊卑之勢日懸，故人主接賢士大夫之時常少，而人臣輔養啓迪之益斯難。惟經筵臨御之時，聖德撝謙，儒臣畢集，於是而稱述往古已然之跡，庶幾感悟觀聽之餘，善可為法，惡可為戒，而於君德治道少有裨補。況茲錄也，考古証今，聞見甚博，挈綱提領，觀聽不勞，以之進讀，如朱子之意，奚為不可？此固執事廟堂事也。愚生草茅，竊有志焉久矣。儻與其進，願執是以從，而猶未之敢也。

translation_en:
…in cunning deceit and harsh scrutiny [?], but understands the Way and righteousness, recognizes security and peril, distinguishes the worthy from the foolish, and discerns right from wrong: thus his wisdom grows broad. He does not esteem violence or overbearing severity, yet the wicked cannot mislead him and flatterers cannot sway him: thus his martial resolve is established. Will not the enterprise of dynastic restoration shine all the more brightly? This is surely what you, honored Examiner, intend.

I have also humbly heard that, since the age when enlightened rulers and worthy ministers encountered one another has grown distant, the gulf in standing between superior and subordinate has widened daily. Thus the ruler seldom has time to meet worthy scholar-officials, and it becomes difficult for his ministers to benefit him through cultivation and instruction. Only when he attends the Classics Colloquium does His Majesty display his sagely humility while the Confucian ministers gather together. There they recount the deeds of antiquity, hoping that what he sees and hears will move him to understanding, so that good deeds may serve as models and evil deeds as warnings, and that they may contribute something to the ruler’s virtue and the Way of governance.

Moreover, this record examines antiquity to verify the present, drawing on extensive learning and experience. It brings out the main principles and essential points without taxing the eyes or ears. Why should it not be presented for reading before the throne, in accordance with Master Zhu’s intention? This is indeed a matter for you in the high councils of government. I, a humble student outside official life, have privately cherished this aspiration for a long time. If permitted to advance, I would wish to bring this proposal with me and follow your lead; yet I have not dared to do so.

論議論中亦復叙事一氣輸瀉幅尺各有結煞末復

廷劾四事為可復而又以董狐南史汲黯宣秉四子為可法其識
卓然足備

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
停滯而其意躍然非有素蘊於中詎能言至此邪
有任人之誠而後官守得盡其職有待人
之恕而後言責得盡其忠盖君舉必書史
之職也有過必諫臣之分也公萬世之是
非勸懲繫焉正一時之得失治忽繇焉故
必得人而後克稱其職雖或得人而任之
不誠待之不恕則有官守者失其職有言
責者不得言矣亦何益於天下國家之事
也哉執事發策以史職言官為問請先述
===
往事而後及我
國朝之盛可乎粵自制書契以来黃帝有蒼
頡夏有終古商有高勢皆史職也然世不
易業如周之史佚魯之史克晋之史蘇史
黯史趙史墨皆世掌之周禮所謂太史掌
六典法則内史掌八枋詔王治小史掌邦
國之志外史掌書外令戴記云天子言則
左史書之動則右史書之厥任亦云重矣
至漢始以太史專占候以他官領修撰又

translation_en:
…without faltering, while its meaning springs vividly forth. Without learning long cultivated within, how could he write so well?

Only when appointments are made with sincerity can officeholders fully discharge their duties; only when men are treated with forbearance can those responsible for remonstrance fully express their loyalty. To record every action of the ruler is the historian’s duty; to remonstrate whenever there is a fault is the minister’s obligation. Impartially judging right and wrong for all ages is what encouragement and admonition depend upon; correcting the successes and failures of the present is what determines good government or disorder. Thus, suitable men must be found before these duties can be properly fulfilled. Even if suitable men are found, unless they are entrusted sincerely and treated with forbearance, officeholders will fail in their duties and those responsible for remonstrance will be unable to speak. What benefit could this possibly bring to the affairs of the realm and the state? You, honored examiners, have posed a policy question concerning historical offices and remonstrance officials. May I first recount earlier events and then turn to the flourishing achievements of our own dynasty?

Ever since writing was devised, the Yellow Emperor had Cang Jie, the Xia had Zhong Gu, and the Shang had Gao Shi [?], all holding historical offices. Their families did not change occupations from generation to generation: Shi Yi of Zhou, Shi Ke of Lu, and Shi Su, Shi An, Shi Zhao, and Shi Mo of Jin all held these responsibilities hereditarily. As described in the Rites of Zhou, the Grand Scribe was responsible for the six canons, laws, and regulations; the Inner Scribe administered the eight powers and advised the king on government; the Assistant Scribe maintained the records of the states; and the Outer Scribe was responsible for writing commands issued outside the court. The Record of Rites compiled by Dai states: “When the Son of Heaven spoke, the Scribe of the Left recorded it; when he acted, the Scribe of the Right recorded it.” Their responsibilities were indeed weighty. Only under the Han was the Grand Scribe assigned exclusively to divination and celestial observation, while other officials were put in charge of historical compilation; furthermore…

…They also separately established five historians “below the pillars” and court diaries within the palace. Sima Qian was the son of Sima Tan, and Ban Gu was the son of Ban Biao. Wei Shu had charge of books and documents for forty years and served as a historiographer for twenty-three; Liu Zhiji served for thirty years, and Jiang Yi [?] for twenty. These arrangements still retained something of the ancient spirit. Emperor Taizong of Tang ordered the Court Diarist, the Court Diary Recorder, and the historiographers to enter daily with the ceremonial guard and attend to recording events. Thus the records of the Zhenguan reign are the most detailed. His only mistake was to inspect the historical record himself, thereby setting a precedent. Later, Li Yifu and Xu Jingzong ordered the historians all to withdraw when the ceremonial guard withdrew, not wishing them to hear the memorials and requests presented to the throne. Yao Shu requested that the chief councilors themselves compile the Record of Current Government. Worse still, supervisors of compilation and superintendents were appointed, and the historians relied solely on reports submitted by the various offices, not daring to record what they themselves saw and heard. Worse again, some were appointed and dismissed in rapid succession; the academy and library posts all became honorary appointments, and men were chosen for their agreement with those in power. Thus Cai Jing became Left Court Diarist, Cai Bian Right Court Diarist, Lin Xi Editorial Director, and Feng Ji Assistant Editorial Director. Private interests proliferated, merely leaving the historical record confused and misleading for all ages.
Ouyang Xiu said: “The academies and libraries are places for cultivating a reserve of talent. title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
素養無以重國使二公而非賢臣則已如
其賢也其言豈不為有見乎嘅自堯舜禹
以来置諫鼓立謗木懸五樂皆求言也然
不以諫名官故工誦箴諫瞽誦詩諫公卿
比諫士傳言諫庶人謗商旅議皆得聴之
周禮所謂師氏以媺詔王曰保氏掌諫王

punctuated: 素養，無以重國。使二公而非賢臣則已，如其賢也，其言豈不為有見乎？嘅！自堯舜禹以来，置諫鼓，立謗木，懸五樂，皆求言也。然不以諫名官，故工誦箴諫，瞽誦詩諫，公卿比諫，士傳言諫，庶人謗，商旅議，皆得聴之。《周禮》所謂師氏以媺詔王，曰保氏掌諫王惡，司諫掌糾萬民，御史賛治書令，厥職亦云異矣。至漢，因秦制，置諫大夫及御史大夫、中丞。唐置左右補闕、拾遺，宋改左右司諫、正言。然或命大夫、中丞與百官絕席，使百官避道；或丞相相與避；或諫官随宰相入閤議事，有失輒奏；或御史言事不先白大夫、中丞，亦甚為崇重。惟姚崇遷李義為美官，而實奪之權；張說出崔沔於外州，而得行其計；李逢吉除韓愈京尹，詔不臺叅，以激李紳而使之相攻；李林甫專進諂諛之徒，公指立仗馬以諷近臣。甚者，六察所言行於有司而不及二府，諫官隸中書門
translation_en:
…without nurturing men of learning beforehand, there is no means of lending weight to the state. If these two gentlemen were not worthy ministers, we might let the matter rest; but if they were worthy, surely their words showed insight? Alas! From the time of Yao, Shun, and Yu, drums for remonstrance were installed, posts for criticism erected, and five musical instruments suspended—all to solicit counsel. Yet no offices were named specifically for remonstrance. Thus musicians recited admonitions to remonstrate; blind musicians recited poems to remonstrate; dukes and ministers remonstrated collectively; officers conveyed words of remonstrance; commoners voiced criticism; and merchants and travelers offered their views. All could be heard. As the Rituals of Zhou says, the Mentor instructed the king through examples of excellence; it says that the Guardian was charged with remonstrating against the king’s faults, the Remonstrator with correcting the myriad people, and the Censor with assisting in the administration of written commands. Their duties were indeed distinct.

Under the Han, following Qin institutions, Grand Masters of Remonstrance were appointed, along with a Censor-in-chief and a Palace Assistant Censor-in-chief. The Tang established Reminders and Omissioners of the Left and Right; the Song changed these to Remonstrators and Rectifiers of Omissions of the Left and Right. Sometimes the Censor-in-chief and Palace Assistant Censor-in-chief were ordered to sit apart from the other officials, and the officials were required to yield the road to them; sometimes even the chief ministers yielded to them. Sometimes remonstrance officials accompanied the chief ministers into the inner hall to deliberate on affairs and immediately submitted a memorial whenever something was amiss. Sometimes censors spoke on affairs without first reporting to the Censor-in-chief or Palace Assistant Censor-in-chief. These offices were thus accorded very great esteem.

Yet Yao Chong promoted Li Yi [?] to an attractive office while actually stripping him of his authority; Zhang Yue sent Cui Mian out to a provincial prefecture and thereby managed to carry out his designs; Li Fengji appointed Han Yu Metropolitan Prefect and secured an edict exempting him from paying a formal visit to the Censorate, thereby provoking Li Shen and causing the two to attack each other. Li Linfu advanced only flatterers and publicly pointed to the horses standing in the ceremonial guard as a veiled warning to the ruler’s close ministers. Worse still, the pronouncements of the six censorial surveillance offices applied to the responsible administrative offices but did not reach the two chief councils, while remonstrance officials were subordinate to the Secretariat–Chancellery…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
下而徒為具員又其甚聚不言是非者在
朝廷擇不敢言人過者為臺諫欲言一事
去一人必多方為計而後敢言言且不盡
如朱子當時之論風節蕩然趨和一時而
已蘇軾曰擢用臺諫固未必皆賢所言亦
未必皆是然須養其鋭氣而借之重權將
以折姦臣之萌而救內重之弊吕祖謙曰
蕭望之遷諫議出補郡守且謂憂其末而
忘其本盖朝無諍臣則不知過是知臺諫
===
之選不容少緩使二公而皆庸人則已如
其非也其言豈不為可信乎愚也竊聞我
聖朝初置翰林院修撰編修檢討為史官别有
起居注至洪武十四年罷而復置永樂間
始罷之或有謂今
丹陛之側石室尚存其儲養造就則洪武癸
丑命編修王連等十人入
禁中
文華堂肄業永樂甲申選進士及修撰曾棨

punctuated:
下，而徒為具員。又其甚，聚不言是非者在朝廷，擇不敢言人過者為臺諫。欲言一事、去一人，必多方為計而後敢言，言且不盡。如朱子當時之論，風節蕩然，趨和一時而已。蘇軾曰：「擢用臺諫，固未必皆賢，所言亦未必皆是，然須養其鋭氣而借之重權，將以折姦臣之萌而救內重之弊。」吕祖謙曰：「蕭望之遷諫議，出補郡守。」且謂：「憂其末而忘其本，盖朝無諍臣則不知過。」是知臺諫之選不容少緩。使二公而皆庸人則已，如其非也，其言豈不為可信乎？
愚也竊聞，我聖朝初置翰林院修撰、編修、檢討為史官，别有起居注，至洪武十四年罷而復置，永樂間始罷之。或有謂今丹陛之側石室尚存。其儲養造就，則洪武癸丑，命編修王連等十人入禁中文華堂肄業；永樂甲申，選進士及修撰曾棨
translation_en:
…Chancellery, and merely filled their posts. Worse still, those who would not discuss right and wrong were gathered at court, and those who dared not speak of others’ faults were chosen as censors and remonstrance officials. To raise a single matter or remove a single person, they had to devise elaborate plans before daring to speak, and even then they did not say everything. As Master Zhu observed at the time, moral courage and integrity had vanished; they merely sought to go along with the prevailing mood. Su Shi said: “Those promoted to serve as censors and remonstrance officials are certainly not necessarily all worthy, nor is everything they say necessarily right. Nevertheless, their vigor must be nurtured and substantial authority entrusted to them, so that they may check treacherous ministers at their first emergence and remedy the abuses of excessive power within the court.” Lü Zuqian said: “Xiao Wangzhi was transferred to the post of Grand Master of Remonstrance, then sent out to serve as a commandery governor.” He further observed: “This is to worry about the branches while forgetting the root, for without ministers who remonstrate, the court cannot recognize its faults.” Thus we know that the selection of censors and remonstrance officials admits of no delay. If these two gentlemen were both mediocre men, we might leave it at that; but if they were not, should their words not be considered trustworthy?
I have humbly heard that, at the beginning of our sagely dynasty, Senior Compilers, Junior Compilers, and Examining Editors of the Hanlin Academy were appointed as historiographers, and that there were separately Court Diarists. These posts were abolished in the fourteenth year of Hongwu and then restored; only during the Yongle reign were they finally abolished. Some say that the stone chamber beside the vermilion palace steps still survives today. As for nurturing and training this body of talent, in the guichou year of Hongwu, Junior Compiler Wang Lian and nine others were ordered to enter Wenhua Hall within the palace to pursue their studies. In the jiashen year of Yongle, metropolitan graduates (jinshi) and Senior Compiler Zeng Qi were selected…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
等二十九人就
文淵閣進學又
簡命編修等官於
內閣參預機務是
祖宗之所以待史職者不為不重矣初罷中書
省改六部并不復置諫官惟設六科都左
右給事中職專封駁糾劾設都察院都御
史及十三道監察御史不繫之院以寓得
自彈糾之意是
===
祖宗之所以待言路者亦不為不重矣仰惟我
聖天子在位崇獎儒臣優納臺諫寸長在所必
錄片善在所必與海內喁喁方拭目以觀
太平之盛而執事猶以盡職盡言望之愚
也患不得人焉爾如得其人則以
宵旰勵精之志
羨墻繼述之思如所謂紀注儲養及封駁
廷劾之制有不可復者乎夫曰得人云者史
臣必節義為上文學次之如董狐之書法

羹墻繼述之思如所謂紀注儲養及封駁
廷劾之制有不可復者乎夫曰得人云者史
臣必節義爲上文學次之如董狐之書法
punctuated:
等二十九人就文淵閣進學，又簡命編修等官於內閣參預機務，是祖宗之所以待史職者不為不重矣。初罷中書省，改六部，并不復置諫官，惟設六科都、左、右給事中，職專封駁糾劾；設都察院都御史及十三道監察御史，不繫之院，以寓得自彈糾之意，是祖宗之所以待言路者亦不為不重矣。
仰惟我聖天子在位，崇獎儒臣，優納臺諫，寸長在所必錄，片善在所必與。海內喁喁，方拭目以觀太平之盛，而執事猶以盡職盡言望之。愚也患不得人焉爾。如得其人，則以宵旰勵精之志、羨墻繼述之思，如所謂紀注儲養及封駁廷劾之制，有不可復者乎？夫曰得人云者，史臣必節義為上，文學次之，如董狐之書法
translation_en:
…and others, twenty-nine men in all, to pursue further study in the Wenyuan Pavilion. They also selected compilers and other officials to participate in confidential state affairs in the Grand Secretariat. Thus the importance our imperial ancestors accorded the historiographical offices was considerable. At the outset, they abolished the Secretariat, reorganized the Six Ministries, and ceased appointing remonstrance officials. They established only chief, left, and right supervising secretaries in the Six Offices of Scrutiny, specifically charged with returning edicts for reconsideration and correcting and impeaching officials. They established censors-in-chief in the Censorate and investigating censors of the Thirteen Circuits, without subordinating the latter to the Censorate, intending thereby to allow them to impeach and correct officials independently. Thus the importance our imperial ancestors accorded the channels for official criticism was also considerable.
I respectfully reflect that our sage Son of Heaven, during his reign, has honored and encouraged scholar-officials and graciously received the counsel of censors and remonstrators. He invariably recognizes even the smallest merit and approves even the slightest good. All within the seas look eagerly forward, clearing their eyes to behold the splendor of an age of great peace. Yet you, honored examiners, still expect officials to discharge their duties fully and speak their minds without reserve. My humble concern is simply that suitable men may not be found. If suitable men are obtained, then, given His Majesty’s resolve to labor diligently from before dawn until late in the evening, and his longing for his forebears [?] and desire to carry on their work, could any of the aforementioned institutions—recording the sovereign’s activities, cultivating future officials, returning edicts for reconsideration, and presenting impeachments at court—not be restored? As for what is meant by obtaining suitable men: among historiographers, integrity and righteousness must rank first, and literary learning second, as exemplified by Dong Hu’s manner of recording events…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
不隠南史之執簡以往可也劉知幾所須
才學識三長者其亦末也爾矣臺諫必威
望為先彈劾次之如汲黯之淮南寢謀宣
秉之百僚敬憚可也司馬光所擇不愛富
貴重惜名節暁知治體三事者斯亦稱也
爾矣末學僭狂不知忌諱惟執事恕而教
之
第四問
左鎰
===
同考試官主事李批道出於天者故不變不
變故亡弊救者時之變非道之變也三代之異尚因
時以捄其弊者也非變乎道也此作能明乎道而於
諸儒之同異得失又能以道而正其是非則可謂知
道矣若此者豈非有道之士乎夫誰舍子
同考試官署郎中高批三代異尚論者紛囂雖
博辯如宋蘇氏立言且不免疵子能言之如是通
達國體實屬望焉
同考試官都給事中蔡批聖人制治趨時而已或

不隠，南史之執簡以往，可也。劉知幾所須才、學、識三長者，其亦末也爾矣。臺諫必威望為先，彈劾次之。如汲黯之淮南寢謀，宣秉之百僚敬憚，可也。司馬光所擇不愛富貴、重惜名節、暁知治體三事者，斯亦稱也爾矣。末學僭狂，不知忌諱，惟執事恕而教之。

第四問
左鎰

同考試官主事李批：道出於天者，故不變；不變，故亡弊。救者，時之變，非道之變也。三代之異尚，因時以捄其弊者也，非變乎道也。此作能明乎道，而於諸儒之同異得失，又能以道而正其是非，則可謂知道矣。若此者，豈非有道之士乎？夫誰舍子？

同考試官署郎中高批：三代異尚，論者紛囂，雖博辯如宋蘇氏，立言且不免疵。子能言之如是，通達國體，實屬望焉。

同考試官都給事中蔡批：聖人制治，趨時而已。或
translation_en:
…concealed nothing in his historical writing, or the Grand Historian of the South, who took up his writing tablets and went forward: such men would suffice. The three strengths Liu Zhiji required—talent, learning, and judgment—are merely secondary. For censorial and remonstrance officials, prestige and authority must come first, and impeachment second. Men like Ji An, whose presence caused the prince of Huainan to abandon his plot, or Xuan Bing, whom the assembled officials respected and feared, would suffice. The three qualities Sima Guang sought—having no love of wealth and rank, deeply cherishing one’s reputation and integrity, and understanding the essentials of government—likewise amount merely to fitness for office. I, a poorly learned student, have been presumptuous and rash, heedless of taboos. I ask only that you forgive and instruct me.

Fourth Question
Zuo Yi

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Bureau Secretary: The Way comes from Heaven and therefore does not change; because it does not change, it has no defects. What requires remedy is change in the times, not change in the Way. The differing preferences of the Three Dynasties were responses to their times, intended to remedy their defects; they were not changes in the Way. This essay clearly understands the Way. Moreover, in considering the agreements and disagreements, successes and errors of the various Confucian scholars, it uses the Way to determine what is right and wrong. Its author may thus be said to understand the Way. Is such a person not a scholar who possesses the Way? Who else but you?

Comment by Associate Examiner Gao, Acting Bureau Director: Discussion of the differing preferences of the Three Dynasties has been clamorous and confused. Even someone as learned and eloquent as Master Su of the Song could not avoid flaws in his pronouncements. Since you can discuss the matter in this fashion, I place real hopes in your thorough understanding of the principles of statecraft.

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
者拘於循環之說牽合支離殊無定論獨此作辨究
明白足破群疑末復以崇質為言尤見深識
同考試官修撰倫批前人亦論及此未下斷
案聞吾子之論不覺洒然後之君子將亦有合乎
考試官學士郭批三尚之說相傳已久子獨
能推原本始以破其非且於古聖王應時為治之意
發揮甚明盖識治體而有卓見者
考試官學士張批問意渾涵對者多勦陳言
泛論訖無定見是作獨能發前人之所未發且於治
===
體若深有意焉可謂有本之學矣
聖人之制治於天下也時焉而已矣時也
者視天下之勢之所趨而為之所者也時
之義不明而世以為狥天下之所趨而已
勢之所趨此重則彼輕彼興則此廢是故
勢有所必廢政有所必興勢有所必趨政

…hemp cloth in summer and furs in winter: only then is this called acting in accordance with the times; no one says that such people oppose Heaven. Thus, those who do not investigate the reasons for adaptation and change, or understand when to exercise restraint and when to allow freedom, but merely follow the tendencies of the world, are like people who wear furs in summer and hemp cloth in winter. At the height of the Three Dynasties, sage kings arose in succession to respond to changes throughout the realm. We have never heard that they maintained any fixed preference: they simply acted according to the times. The claim that the Xia prized wholehearted sincerity, the Shang unadorned substance, and the Zhou cultural refinement was probably a late formulation of the school of the Zhu and Si rivers. These were not designations originally used by the Three Dynasties themselves. Later scholars traced apparent similarities in their customs and forcibly applied these labels to their governments.

The “Record of Exemplary Conduct” (Biaoji) says: “The refinement of Yu and Xia did not surpass their substance; the substance of Shang and Zhou did not surpass their refinement.” If we accept these words, we may say that Xia emphasized substance and Shang refinement. It also says: “The way of Xia was close to the people and marked by wholehearted sincerity; its people's failing was to be rustic and lacking in refinement. The people of Zhou were close to the people and marked by wholehearted sincerity; their people's failing was to be refined yet without shame.” If we accept these words, we may also say that Zhou prized wholehearted sincerity. The words of the “Record of Exemplary Conduct” did not necessarily come from Kongzi, yet later accounts of the Three Dynasties’ differing preferences have generally followed them.

Master Dong advised Emperor Wu of Han to curtail Zhou practices and adopt those of Xia. The grouping together of wholehearted sincerity, reverence, and refinement actually began with him. The historian Sima Qian probably heard his theory of the cyclical succession of the kingly Way from Master Dong. 質者實自此始漢後諸儒習其讀而混其
傳於是忠質文之說至今沿之然則尚質
尚敬之異可以無辨也忠之與質則朱子
辨之明矣而亦可以無容辨也所急者其
惟審治體已乎愚以為天下古今之變文

…“altered the refinement of Zhou and followed the simplicity of Yin.” This explanation has no basis in the canonical texts, yet the claim that Shang prized simplicity actually began here. Scholars after the Han grew accustomed to this reading and confused its transmission; thus the theory of loyalty, simplicity, and refinement has been perpetuated to this day. The difference between prizing simplicity and prizing reverence therefore need not be debated. As for loyalty and simplicity, Master Zhu has clearly distinguished them, so further debate is likewise unnecessary. Surely the urgent task is simply to understand the essentials of governance!

In my humble view, refinement and simplicity encompass all changes in the world, past and present. Understanding the essentials of governance comes down entirely to timeliness; and the significance of timeliness comes down entirely to refinement and simplicity. Why is this? The world has existed for a long time. From primordial antiquity down to Huangdi, Yao, and Shun, prevailing customs gradually developed and human culture gradually became manifest. Not a day passed without the world moving toward refinement. This was the natural tendency of circumstances and the necessary outcome of principle. Compared with the earlier age of knotted cords, Yu and Xia were already refined; compared with the later Shang and Zhou, Yu and Xia were already simple. Refinement and simplicity are defined in relation to one another, and together encompass all changes in the course of the world. What need is there to speak of loyalty and reverence?

During the decline of Xia and Shang, the world sank daily into superficiality and extravagance. How could there have been the supposed popular failings of rusticity and preoccupation with spirits [?]? King Wu reversed Shang’s government, conducting government according to the old ways; from this we can understand how Tang continued Yu’s work. Both brought things back from refinement to simplicity. How could there have been any supposed remedying of rusticity through reverence, or of preoccupation with spirits through refinement? The refinement of middle antiquity reached its height in the time of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, when they could not but institute for it…

事制而曲防於是繁文縟禮生焉雖然為
之度數品節期使天下無過乎此而已矣
誠知天下之文不可勝捄而質不可以卒
復故以夫聖人之質而約天下之文庶幾
可以久存而無敝天下習見其文而遂以
為尚文不亦惑乎隄之防水期於無决幸
而無决則指隄以為導水也嗟乎水既自
導矣天下既自文矣雖聖人將若之何武
王周公之不以文率天下亦明矣夫子之

…to regulate each matter and guard against every contingency; thus elaborate forms and intricate rites arose. Yet their establishment of measures, gradations, and distinctions aimed only to keep the world from exceeding these bounds. They truly understood that the world's excesses of refinement could not all be remedied, and that simplicity could not be restored at once. They therefore used the sages’ own simplicity to restrain the world's refinement, hoping thereby to preserve it long without deterioration. People grew accustomed to seeing these forms and consequently supposed that the sages prized refinement. Was this not a misunderstanding? A dike holds back water with the aim of preventing a breach. If, fortunately, no breach occurs, people point to the dike and suppose that it channels the water onward. Alas! The water was already flowing of itself, and the world was already tending toward refinement of itself. What could even sages do about it? It is thus clear that King Wu and the Duke of Zhou did not lead the world toward refinement.

The word “looked” implies both retention and alteration; “discarded and added” means more than merely increasing embellishment. His praise, “How splendid its culture!” was simply like his praise of Yao: “How radiant were his cultural accomplishments!” How can one invoke the Master's words to claim that Zhou prized refinement? 小變其道不足以捄之故以致用夏忠為
言誠得承救易變之理惜乎武帝好文之
心勝而莫能用也遷也謂世道循環則可
謂王道循環則不可草昧之初天地既物
生民虔劉智勇俱盡碩果不食真精再完
若一小開闢然此文復為質之機也吾知
===
時者及是時而保合太和使天下無失其
質而可矣然而不十數年而天下又已胃
趨於文矣故夫世道之循環自文而質者
不十一而自質而文者常十九也敦質以
約文猶懼其不勝而又奚循環之有乎彼
蘇子者有見於時變無見於治體是周人
之餘救也彼亦見夫禮樂教化之不興民
俗之不善故激焉而為是言夫民俗之不
善是文之漓非質之救也禮樂教化之興
punctuated:
君眩名失實，以亡於秦。秦以文法持天下，其敝，上下文具相應，無惻隱之實，卒離其民，以亡於漢。文勝之弊，一至此也。董生謂小變其道不足以捄之，故以致用夏忠為言，誠得承敝易變之理。惜乎武帝好文之心勝，而莫能用也。
遷也謂世道循環則可，謂王道循環則不可。草昧之初，天地改物，生民虔劉，智勇俱盡，碩果不食，真精再完，若一小開闢然，此文復為質之機也。善知時者，及是時而保合太和，使天下無失其質而可矣。然而不十數年，而天下又已日趨於文矣。故夫世道之循環，自文而質者不十一，而自質而文者常十九也。敦質以約文，猶懼其不勝，而又奚循環之有乎？
彼蘇子者，有見於時變，無見於治體，是周人之餘敝也。彼亦見夫禮樂教化之不興，民俗之不善，故激焉而為是言。夫民俗之不善，是文之漓，非質之敝也。禮樂教化之興，
translation_en:
…rulers were dazzled by names and lost sight of substance, and thus fell to Qin. Qin maintained its rule over the realm through legal formalities. The resulting abuse was that superiors and subordinates answered one another with empty formal observances, without any genuine compassion. In the end, Qin alienated its people and fell to Han. Such were the extremes to which the predominance of outward refinement led. Master Dong held that slight changes to this approach would not suffice to remedy it, and therefore advocated putting the wholehearted sincerity of Xia into practice. He truly grasped the principle of making changes to remedy inherited abuses. Regrettably, Emperor Wu’s fondness for outward refinement prevailed, and he could not put this counsel into practice.
For Sima Qian to say that the course of the world moves in cycles is permissible; to say that the Way of the true king moves in cycles is not. At the outset of an unsettled age, heaven and earth undergo transformation, the people are slaughtered, and the resources of wisdom and courage alike are exhausted. Yet the great fruit remains uneaten, and the true vital essence becomes whole again, as though heaven and earth had undergone a minor re-creation. This is the moment when outward refinement returns to native substance. Those who understand the times well need only preserve supreme harmony at this juncture and ensure that the realm does not lose its native substance. Yet before even ten or so years have passed, the realm is already tending daily toward outward refinement again. Thus, in the cycles of worldly affairs, transitions from outward refinement to native substance account for fewer than one in ten, while those from native substance to outward refinement regularly account for nine in ten. Even when we strengthen native substance to restrain outward refinement, we still fear that it will not prevail. What grounds, then, are there for speaking of a cycle?
That Master Su perceived changes in the times but failed to perceive the essential principles of government: this was a lingering failing inherited from the people of Zhou. He too saw that rites, music, and moral instruction were not flourishing and that popular customs were poor; provoked by this, he made such statements. But poor popular customs result from the dilution of refinement, not from the failings of native substance. As for the flourishing of rites, music, and moral instruction…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
有質有文而質為之本揭文之名以興禮
樂教化無怪乎文日浮而俗日偷也武王
周公盖將求虞夏之質而不能今則曰虞
夏求周之文而未至非所以為法何其昧
於時義而敢於誣民哉由是觀之三代盛
王皆未嘗有所定尚稽古制治則不可以
無所定尚審尚莫過乎觀時觀時莫過乎
尚質酌古準今雖百世可知也執事之問
其有斯世之隱憂乎承平百年恬嬉成風
===
文勝質衰時勢則有然者是故條章政教
良法美意一一具存而承流宣化者各以
其意為治情隔澤壅不信於民士大夫議
論常依名節而行己臨民多與言鑿心迹
之判若秦越然斯二者其來甚久而將來
為患甚深天下利病未易悉數然使二弊
不除則雖日陳百害日畫百利秪益為虛
文而已漢宣之政未及乎化民成俗之務
徒以綜核名實之效能使漢道赫然中興

punctuated:
有質有文，而質為之本。揭文之名以興禮樂教化，無怪乎文日浮而俗日偷也。武王、周公盖將求虞夏之質而不能，今則曰虞夏求周之文而未至，非所以為法，何其昧於時義而敢於誣民哉！由是觀之，三代盛王皆未嘗有所定尚。稽古制治，則不可以無所定尚。審尚莫過乎觀時，觀時莫過乎尚質。酌古準今，雖百世可知也。

執事之問，其有斯世之隱憂乎？承平百年，恬嬉成風，文勝質衰，時勢則有然者。是故條章政教、良法美意，一一具存，而承流宣化者各以其意為治，情隔澤壅，不信於民。士大夫議論常依名節，而行己臨民多與言鑿，心迹之判若秦越然。斯二者，其來甚久，而將來為患甚深。天下利病，未易悉數，然使二弊不除，則雖日陳百害，日畫百利，秪益為虛文而已。漢宣之政，未及乎化民成俗之務，徒以綜核名實之效，能使漢道赫然中興。
translation_en:
…has both substance and refinement, with substance as its foundation. If one promotes ritual, music, and moral instruction under the banner of refinement, it is no wonder that refinement grows daily more superficial and customs daily more lax. King Wu and the Duke of Zhou presumably sought to attain the substance of the ages of Yu and Xia but could not. Yet now it is said that Yu and Xia sought Zhou’s refinement but had not attained it, and thus cannot serve as models. How blind to what the times require, and how bold in misleading the people! Viewed in this light, the sage kings of the Three Dynasties never maintained any fixed preference. Yet when drawing upon antiquity to establish government, one cannot dispense with a settled preference. To determine what to favor, nothing is better than examining the times; in examining the times, nothing is better than favoring substance. By weighing antiquity against the present, one may know even what lies a hundred generations ahead.

Does your question, honored examiner, express an unspoken anxiety about this age? After a century of peace, complacency and indulgence have become customary; refinement prevails while substance declines. The circumstances of the times have indeed brought this about. Thus regulations, governmental measures, and moral instruction—all the fine laws and good intentions—remain fully in place. Yet those charged with transmitting imperial influence and spreading moral transformation govern each according to his own wishes. The people’s circumstances are shut off from those above, imperial beneficence is obstructed, and the people have no trust in government. In their discussions, scholar-officials constantly invoke reputation and integrity, but in their personal conduct and administration of the people they often contradict their words [?]. Their inner intentions and outward deeds are as far apart as Qin and Yue. These two failings have existed for a very long time and will cause very grave harm in the future. The benefits and afflictions of the realm cannot readily be enumerated in full. But unless these two failings are removed, even if we daily set forth a hundred harms and devise a hundred beneficial measures, we shall merely add to empty formalities. Emperor Xuan of Han’s government did not extend to the work of transforming the people and establishing good customs. Yet merely through the effectiveness of comprehensively checking actual performance against professed claims, he was able to bring about a resplendent restoration of Han rule…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
後世人主以尚質之心行核實之政亦何
王道之不可舉哉方今
聖主臨御厲精圖理敦儉朴以為天下先躬農
桑以為天下勸用人則必察言觀行取士
則必崇雅黜浮意將復虞夏之質追隆古
之風賢公卿百執事各以其職贊襄於下
其於時義之要王道之端蓋必講之熟矣
愚不敏所願勵行復言仰裨萬一樂觀
德化之成區區董生之論又惡足為獻哉
===
第五問
蔣信
同考試官主事林 批 理財一策夫人能言之
而掇拾成說殊多浮泛此篇以富民富國剖析漢隋
脩短至於積穀之議不謂其不可行而在乎賢有司
真確論也錄之以見經濟之學
同考試官給事中葉 批 言富國必本之厚下此
固不易之論而語意懇至可以動觀者為民之心矣
同考試官編修程 批 富國富民辯之了了蓋

同考試官主事林批：理財一策，夫人能言之，而掇拾成說，殊多浮泛。此篇以富民富國剖析漢隋脩短，至於積穀之議，不謂其不可行，而在乎賢有司，真確論也。錄之以見經濟之學。

translation_en:
If rulers of later ages governed by scrutinizing actual performance, with a mind that prized substance, why could the Kingly Way not be put into practice? Now our sagely sovereign occupies the throne, exerting himself wholeheartedly in pursuit of good government. He upholds frugality and simplicity as an example to all under Heaven, and personally performs the rites of agriculture and sericulture to encourage the realm. In employing men, he invariably examines their words and observes their conduct; in selecting scholars, he invariably honors what is correct and refined and rejects the superficial. His intention is to restore the substance of the ages of Shun and Xia and recover the customs of high antiquity. Worthy dukes, ministers, and the hundred officials assist him from below, each through his own office. Surely they have thoroughly considered the essential requirements of the times and the foundations of the Kingly Way. Dull and untalented as I am, I wish only to strive in conduct and make good my words, contributing even the smallest assistance to His Majesty and rejoicing to witness the fulfillment of his moral transformation of the people. How could Master Dong’s modest argument be worthy of presentation?

Fifth Question
Jiang Xin

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Bureau Secretary: Everyone can speak about the policy of managing finances, but those who merely gather received opinions are all too often superficial and vague. This essay distinguishes between enriching the people and enriching the state to analyze the strengths and weaknesses of the Han and Sui. As for the proposal to accumulate grain, it does not declare it impracticable, but holds that its success depends upon worthy officials in charge. This is a truly sound judgment. It is included to demonstrate learning in statecraft.

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
籌國至計也錄之豈徒以其辭焉已哉
同考試官編修張批議論平實文有條理可
以觀子用世矣
考試官學士郭批以儉修訂二君之得失以仁
義為理財之中正蓋知言者也
考試官學士張批以富民富國評品二代最為
有見終篇所論蓋亦深體事情者
善富國者能忘天下之利而後能享天下
之大利人孰不知國以財為利也而不知
===
國之所由以敝者亦財也夫惟知財之有
利於國而又知國之為利有不盡出於財
則凡可以忘利而厚民者固有道矣其為
利也孰大於此於乎此富國富民之所由
分而人主善擇術者之所宜審也今日
國家之政莫急於財不猶有可得而論之者
乎宜勤執事之間也蓋嘗聞之先王之御
天下也量地以制邑量邑以居人辨土地
之宜料山澤之利然皆因其所利而勸之

善富國者，能忘天下之利，而後能享天下之大利。人孰不知國以財為利也，而不知國之所由以敝者亦財也。夫惟知財之有利於國，而又知國之為利有不盡出於財，則凡可以忘利而厚民者，固有道矣。其為利也，孰大於此？於乎！此富國富民之所由分，而人主善擇術者之所宜審也。今日國家之政，莫急於財，不猶有可得而論之者乎？宜勤執事之間也。蓋嘗聞之，先王之御天下也，量地以制邑，量邑以居人，辨土地之宜，料山澤之利，然皆因其所利而勸之。

…the foremost plan for managing the state. Could its inclusion here be merely for its literary expression?
Associate Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Compiler, comments: The argument is sound and straightforward, and the writing well ordered. From this one can see your capacity to serve the world.
Examiner Guo, a Hanlin Academician, comments: Using frugality to assess the successes and failures of the two rulers [?], and taking benevolence and righteousness as the proper standard for managing wealth, the author is surely one who understands sound principles.
Examiner Zhang, a Hanlin Academician, comments: The assessment of the two dynasties in terms of enriching the people and enriching the state is particularly perceptive. The arguments throughout the essay show a deep understanding of actual circumstances.
One who excels at enriching the state can set aside the pursuit of profit throughout the realm, and only then enjoy the realm’s greatest benefit. Who does not know that wealth benefits the state? Yet people do not know that wealth is also what brings the state to ruin. If one understands that wealth benefits the state, but also understands that the state’s benefits do not all derive from wealth, then there is indeed a way to set aside profit and improve the people’s livelihood. What benefit could be greater than this? Alas! Here lies the distinction between enriching the state and enriching the people, which a ruler skilled in choosing his methods ought to examine carefully. In the government of our state today, nothing is more urgent than finance. Is there not still something to be said about it? It is fitting to trouble you gentlemen with this inquiry [?]. I have heard that when the former kings governed the realm, they assessed the land to establish settlements, assessed the settlements to accommodate the people, distinguished what the soils were suited to produce, and appraised the resources of mountains and marshes. Yet in all this they encouraged the people in accordance with what benefited them…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
因其所欲而化之如是焉而已矣其取之
於下也謹節以制度謹度以宜民養百官
之政助六軍之功然皆取之有時焉用之
有禮焉各當義而已矣故易曰天地之大
德曰生聖人之大寶曰位何以守位曰仁
何以聚人曰財理財正辭禁民為非曰義
而洪範八政一曰食二曰貨以此見理財
先民食者帝王之要務生人之大經也特
不可使之公私偏病焉耳是故夏后則壤
===
而康歌興魯宣稅畝而王澤竭豈非職此
之故哉三代而下則有可慨矣自漢言之
稱富庶者有文帝焉考之史傳則未見其
能為富國之術者方其即位百務未遑也
春和議貸賜半田租未幾而詔悉除之其
取諸民者可謂至薄矣然終帝之世閭閻
充牣府廩彌殷貫朽粟陳之積至不可殫
紀果何以得此哉亦以帝也寬仁玄默厚
養蒸黎惜中人之產以罷露臺集上書之

取諸民者可謂至薄矣然終帝之世閭閻
充牣府廩彌殷貫朽粟陳之積至不可殫
紀果何以得此哉亦以帝也寬仁玄默厚
養蒸黎惜中人之產罷露臺集上書之
punctuated:
因其所欲而化之，如是焉而已矣。其取之於下也，謹節以制度，謹度以宜民，養百官之政，助六軍之功，然皆取之有時焉，用之有禮焉，各當義而已矣。故《易》曰：「天地之大德曰生，聖人之大寶曰位。何以守位？曰仁。何以聚人？曰財。理財正辭，禁民為非，曰義。」而《洪範》八政，一曰食，二曰貨。以此見理財先民食者，帝王之要務，生人之大經也。特不可使之公私偏病焉耳。是故夏后則壤而康歌興，魯宣稅畝而王澤竭，豈非職此之故哉？
三代而下，則有可慨矣。自漢言之，稱富庶者有文帝焉。考之史傳，則未見其能為富國之術者。方其即位，百務未遑也，春和議貸，賜半田租，未幾而詔悉除之。其取諸民者，可謂至薄矣。然終帝之世，閭閻充牣，府廩彌殷，貫朽粟陳之積，至不可殫紀。果何以得此哉？亦以帝也寬仁玄默，厚養蒸黎，惜中人之產以罷露臺，集上書之
translation_en:
…and guided their transformation in accordance with their desires: that was all. In taking resources from those below, they carefully regulated expenditure through established institutions and carefully set measures suited to the people, supporting the administration of the hundred officials and assisting the work of the six armies. Yet all their levies were taken at the proper times, and all their expenditure accorded with ritual propriety; each simply conformed to righteousness. Thus the Book of Changes says: “The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called giving life; the great treasure of the sage is called his position. By what does he preserve his position? Benevolence. By what does he gather the people? Wealth. Managing wealth, rectifying pronouncements, and prohibiting the people from wrongdoing are called righteousness.” Among the eight affairs of government in the “Great Plan,” the first is food and the second is goods. This shows that managing wealth while giving priority to the people's sustenance is an essential duty of emperors and kings and a fundamental principle for sustaining human life. One must simply ensure that neither public nor private interests suffer disproportionately. Thus, when the rulers of Xia assessed contributions according to the soil, songs of contentment arose; when Duke Xuan of Lu taxed land by the mu, the beneficence of the ancient kings ran dry. Was this not precisely the reason?
After the Three Dynasties, there is much to lament. Speaking of the Han, Emperor Wen was celebrated for wealth and abundance. Yet examining the historical accounts, we find no evidence that he practiced techniques for enriching the state. When he first ascended the throne, he had not yet had leisure to attend to the myriad affairs of government. In the mild spring weather, he deliberated on relief loans [?] and remitted half the land tax; before long, he issued an edict abolishing it altogether. What he took from the people may indeed be called exceedingly little. Yet by the end of his reign, the households were well supplied and the treasuries and granaries increasingly abundant. The accumulated stores, with their rotting strings of cash and aging grain, became too great to record exhaustively. How, indeed, was this achieved? It was also because the emperor was generous and benevolent, reserved and quiet, and generously nurtured the common people. Unwilling to spend the equivalent of an ordinary household's property, he abandoned construction of the Dew Terrace; he collected the [bags used for] submitted memorials…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
囊以為殿帷酒醪有禁重糜穀也力田有
科示敦本也納太息流涕之疏以開直言
敺末技遊食之民盡緣南畝凡其所為皆
一切與民休息之政而又躬行節儉以先
之漢業其有不昌乎其後景武繼之刻薄
任數張大窮兵天下蕭然膏血並竭其不
即危者蒙先帝之澤而未之斬也先儒謂
漢家享國之久皆文帝所留豈不信哉降
是以後稱富庶者有隋文焉考之傳記則
===
未見其能為富民之政者當其在位有司
上計也府蔵盈溢積於廊廡至闢左蔵院
以受之其培諸國者可謂至厚矣胡為開
皇之閒關內民饑山東就食豆屑雜糠之
賤至不能給抑何以至此極哉亦以帝也
險黠忮忍捐棄仁恩河南荆淅皆水則發
丁以築長城河北諸州並饑又舉兵以伐
江左大索貌閱窮戶口也作輸籍法嚴推
校也岐州營繕累歲彌殷三河困窮長安

punctuated:
囊以為殿帷；酒醪有禁，重糜穀也；力田有科，示敦本也。納太息流涕之疏，以開直言；敺末技遊食之民，盡緣南畝。凡其所為，皆一切與民休息之政，而又躬行節儉以先之，漢業其有不昌乎？其後景、武繼之，刻薄任數，張大窮兵，天下蕭然，膏血並竭。其不即危者，蒙先帝之澤而未之斬也。先儒謂漢家享國之久，皆文帝所留，豈不信哉？
降是以後，稱富庶者有隋文焉。考之傳記，則未見其能為富民之政者。當其在位，有司上計也，府蔵盈溢，積於廊廡，至闢左蔵院以受之。其培諸國者，可謂至厚矣。胡為開皇之閒，關內民饑，山東就食，豆屑雜糠之賤，至不能給？抑何以至此極哉？亦以帝也險黠忮忍，捐棄仁恩。河南、荆淅皆水，則發丁以築長城；河北諸州並饑，又舉兵以伐江左。大索貌閱，窮戶口也；作輸籍法，嚴推校也。岐州營繕，累歲彌殷；三河困窮，長安
translation_en:
…bags to make curtains for the palace halls. He restricted alcoholic drinks because he regarded wasting grain as a serious matter; he established distinctions for diligent farmers to demonstrate his commitment to agriculture, the foundation of livelihood. He accepted the memorial expressing deep sighs and flowing tears, thereby encouraging frank speech. He directed people engaged in subsidiary crafts or living idly to take up work in the fields. Everything he did constituted measures that allowed the people respite and recovery, and he personally practiced frugality to set them an example. How could the Han enterprise have failed to flourish? Emperors Jing and Wu succeeded him: harsh and calculating, they pursued aggrandizement and exhausted their resources in warfare. All under Heaven became desolate, and the people's lifeblood was drained away. That the dynasty did not immediately fall into peril was because it still enjoyed the former emperor's beneficence, which had not yet been cut off. Earlier Confucian scholars said that the Han dynasty's long tenure of rule was entirely the legacy of Emperor Wen. Surely this is true!
Among later rulers, Emperor Wen of Sui was acclaimed for wealth and abundance. Yet examining the historical accounts, we find no evidence that he could implement policies to enrich the people. During his reign, when the responsible officials submitted their fiscal accounts, the government storehouses were overflowing, with goods piled up in the corridors, so that an additional compound for the Left Treasury had to be opened to receive them. What he accumulated for the state may indeed be called exceedingly ample. Why, then, during the Kaihuang era, did the people within the passes suffer famine and seek food east of the mountains, unable to obtain even such cheap fare as ground beans mixed with chaff? How could matters have reached such an extreme? It was because the emperor was treacherous, cunning, malicious, and cruel, casting aside benevolence and kindness. When Henan and the Jing and Xi regions were all flooded, he conscripted men to build the Great Wall; when the prefectures of Hebei were all suffering famine, he again raised an army to attack Jiangzuo. He conducted extensive searches and inspections of people's physical appearance to exhaustively register households and individuals. He instituted the tax assessment register system to enforce rigorous scrutiny and checking. Construction works in Qizhou grew ever more extensive year after year; the Sanhe region was impoverished, and Chang'an…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
竟詘凡其所為皆一切與民仇怨之事而
又躬行奢侈以道之隋室其有不敞乎其
後煬帝繼之驕淫縱欲竭澤而漁百姓怨
之盜賊並起其即殞焉者是襲亡周之焰
而復熾之也史稱隋文國計之富非近世
所及果安在哉蓋漢文富民者也忘其利
也隋文富國者也有其利也忘利之效其
利大雖以子孫保之而有餘有利之效其
害深僅以其身守之而不免原其始也皆
===
由擇術之不審以致利害相去之遠若是
耳於乎二君豈惟謀不同術抑時亦有不
同矣何以言之隋文之時喪亂甫平生齒
未復譬之若子初生乳哺而慈煦之猶懼
不祿况可日撻而促之使斃乎漢文之時
則人少壯之日也筋力榮衛日寢以盛而
慈母者又謹察其欲而調娛之則豈有夭
閼者乎傳有之三代而上生民之命制於
君三代而下生民之命制於天夫民須君

punctuated:
竟詘。凡其所為，皆一切與民仇怨之事，而又躬行奢侈以道之，隋室其有不敞乎？其後煬帝繼之，驕淫縱欲，竭澤而漁，百姓怨之，盜賊並起。其即殞焉者，是襲亡周之焰而復熾之也。史稱隋文國計之富，非近世所及，果安在哉？蓋漢文富民者也，忘其利也；隋文富國者也，有其利也。忘利之效，其利大，雖以子孫保之而有餘；有利之效，其害深，僅以其身守之而不免。原其始也，皆由擇術之不審，以致利害相去之遠若是耳。
於乎！二君豈惟謀不同術，抑時亦有不同矣。何以言之？隋文之時，喪亂甫平，生齒未復，譬之若子初生，乳哺而慈煦之，猶懼不祿，况可日撻而促之使斃乎？漢文之時，則人少壯之日也，筋力榮衛日寢以盛，而慈母者又謹察其欲而調娛之，則豈有夭閼者乎？傳有之：「三代而上，生民之命制於君；三代而下，生民之命制於天。」夫民須君
translation_en:
…was ultimately impoverished. Everything he did made him an enemy of the people, and he further set the example by personally indulging in extravagance. How could the Sui ruling house escape ruin [?]? Afterward, Emperor Yang succeeded him. Arrogant and dissolute, he gave free rein to his desires, draining the pond to catch its fish. The common people resented him, and bandits rose everywhere. His swift destruction came from inheriting the flames of the fallen Zhou and fanning them into renewed intensity. The histories claim that the wealth of the state under Emperor Wen of Sui was unmatched in recent ages. Yet where, in the end, was that wealth?
Emperor Wen of Han enriched the people, forgetting his own gain; Emperor Wen of Sui enriched the state, taking its gains for himself. The benefits of forgetting gain were so great that there was more than enough for his descendants to preserve. The harm resulting from appropriating gain was so profound that, even seeking only to maintain his holdings during his own lifetime, he could not escape it. Tracing this back to its beginnings, it all arose from insufficient care in choosing methods of government, causing benefit and harm to diverge so widely.
Alas! These two rulers differed not only in their plans and methods; their times differed as well. How can this be explained? In Emperor Wen of Sui’s time, devastation and disorder had only just been quelled, and the population had not yet recovered. It was like a newborn child: even when nursed, fed, and tenderly warmed, there was still fear that it might die. How could one beat it daily and hasten its death? Emperor Wen of Han’s time, by contrast, was like a person’s vigorous youth. Muscular strength and the nourishing and protective vital forces grew stronger by the day; and a loving mother carefully observed the child’s wishes, tending to its needs and keeping it content. How, then, could its life be cut short?
A transmitted text says: “In the Three Dynasties and earlier, the lives of the people were controlled by the ruler; after the Three Dynasties, the lives of the people were controlled by Heaven.” Now, the people depend upon their ruler…

title: 嘉靖十一年會試錄
text:
以生也至不得已而聽命於天則其政可
知矣斯言也盖所以箴後世之君殖國而
忘民也善乎李翺作平賦書亦曰人知厚
斂之可以富國而不知薄斂之為富愈大
也其真有見於此哉仰惟我
皇上嗣位以来
勤恤民隱躬勸農桑禁吏貪殘形之播告
恩至渥也頃者畿輔之地饑饉相仍川陝之間
煙火幾絶至厪
===
九重之慮大發
内帑之金逋負並蠲民咸蘇息矣執事猶以
公私財用為慮豈非漢文之時猶有過計
如賈誼者乎誼之言曰漢之為漢垂四十
餘年矣公私之財猶可哀痛即不幸有方
二三千里之旱邊警有急國何以待之而
其言一以貯積為主噫誼之言豈可廢哉
今日之事姑以積粟言之司會之臣嘗議
及此矣顧其為策急效而忘遠說者謂一

斂之可以富國而不知薄斂之爲富愈大
